Following Trump's election as US President, the global economy faces greater uncertainty. Not only did the election outcome catch the market by surprise, but the related market reactions were also unexpected. In particular, the expectation that Trump's measures such as tax reform, increased infrastructure spending, and deregulation would boost US economic growth drove global equity markets higher. After the new US administration takes office, US policy direction may undergo fundamental changes in two areas — a shift from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and a shift from globalisation to anti-globalisation — which could have far-reaching implications for the global economic landscape. However, the tax cut measures anticipated by the market may fail to provide the expected stimulus to US economic growth. In particular, with US economic activity now close to its economic potential, fiscal stimulus measures may only bring a mild cyclical boost to US economic growth, while exacerbating the upside risk to US inflation. Although it remains uncertain whether the US Federal Reserve (Fed) will as a result significantly accelerate the pace of monetary policy tightening, long-term bond yields have already risen markedly, partly reflecting market expectations of increasing inflation risks. Meanwhile, the rise of trade protectionism would create a "lose-lose" outcome for the US and the rest of the world. Increased trade barriers would lead to market distortions that harm overall interests, hinder global trade flows, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. At the same time, political instability remains a major risk and adverse factor, particularly for Europe's still-weak economic recovery. As for emerging market economies, the risk of capital outflows resulting from the accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes and further US dollar appreciation has risen. This could weigh on economic growth and intensify the risk of rapid capital outflows. Indeed, amid expectations that the Trump administration would implement large-scale fiscal expansion and concerns over surging energy prices, the market has already repriced inflation risks, causing long-term bond yields to rise significantly and broadly across advanced economies as well as many emerging market economies. The findings show that, since the 2013 "taper tantrum", the influence of the US Treasury bond market on sovereign bond markets has deepened, and that US interest rate hikes and tightening financial conditions would have significant impacts on advanced economies and emerging market economies. In East Asia, economic growth accelerated slightly in the second half of 2016 as exports recovered, but the earlier market volatility—including regional currency depreciation and rising sovereign yields caused by concerns over possible policy changes by the new US administration—only gradually stabilised early this year. Looking ahead, East Asia may maintain steady growth in 2017, but the risks and uncertainties it faces have both increased. US interest rate hikes, regional currency depreciation, and intensifying financial market volatility—these factors may lead to tighter financial conditions. Meanwhile, the US may implement protectionist policies, which could affect regional economies, though the actual impact remains unclear at present. In Mainland China, overall economic growth accelerated slightly in the second half of 2016 amid robust growth in infrastructure investment and improved private sector business spending. Although the economy continued to show signs of stabilisation, uncertainty remains in the Mainland's growth outlook. In particular, given the government's determination to curb rising home prices, if the housing market continues to cool, the real estate sector's contribution to growth this year may diminish. At the same time, the ongoing advancement of economic structural adjustment and changes in China-US trade relations may increase uncertainty in the near-term economic outlook. On the external front, although the renminbi remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) currency basket during the reporting period, capital outflow pressures increased somewhat towards the end of 2016 as the US dollar appreciated and US interest rates rose, and subsequently appeared to ease slightly in early 2017. Although private sector economic activity showed signs of stabilisation, some concerns remained in the market over the effectiveness of monetary policy, particularly given that M1 growth accelerated while M2 growth slowed. Box 2 (see page 24) explores whether the Mainland economy has fallen into a liquidity trap, while Box 3 (see page 27) examines the factors that may have caused the divergence between M1 and M2 growth. The findings indicate that there is no evidence that the Mainland has fallen into a liquidity trap, and that the main reasons M1 grew markedly faster than M2 are that monetary easing in recent years has reduced the opportunity cost of holding liquid money, and that rising economic uncertainty may have increased demand for precautionary money. Hong Kong's economic growth accelerated slightly in the second half of 2016. Quarter-on-quarter real GDP growth rose from 0.8% in the third quarter to 1.2% in the fourth quarter. On the domestic front, private consumption growth continued to strengthen, while buoyant infrastructure activity in the fourth quarter drove investment growth. On the external front, goods export growth rose as regional trade flows improved, while service exports grew steadily as trade-related and transport services recovered. Owing to faster growth in goods and services imports, net exports continued to drag on real GDP growth in the second half of the year. As economic growth picked up, the overall unemployment rate edged down to 3.3% in December. Economic growth in 2017 is expected to remain moderate. The government's and market consensus forecasts for real GDP growth in 2017 are 2-3% and 2.0% respectively. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook still faces significant external headwinds. The protectionist rhetoric of the new US administration has increased the downside risks to global trade and to Hong Kong's external demand. Amid appreciation pressure on the US dollar and expectations of an accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes, the global financial environment is expected to provide less support to the real economy, and could in particular lead to tighter local financial conditions if tail risks materialise. Box 4 (see page 41) discusses the construction of Hong Kong's financial conditions index to help monitor local financial conditions. Since the second half of 2016, local inflationary pressures have remained moderate, while quarter-on-quarter inflation momentum accelerated slightly in the fourth quarter of 2016, mainly due to food price volatility and rising housing rental. As import prices remained stable and domestic cost pressures were moderate, inflationary pressures are expected to remain manageable. Despite market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained largely stable, but occasionally weakened after the US interest rate hike in December. The CUs were not triggered. As the US dollar appreciated, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index rose further. Owing to the sizeable Monetary Base, HIBORs remained low, but have risen since October due to year-end funding demand and catching up with US dollar rate increases. As a result, average mortgage rates, after falling to a recent low of 1.71% in October amid intense competition in the mortgage lending business, edged up slightly to 2.07% in January 2017. Overall loan growth accelerated to 4.2% in the second half of 2016, compared with 2.2% growth in the first half. The growth was supported by strengthening local economic activity and rising financing needs of multinational corporations at year-end. Domestic loan growth accelerated slightly, while loans used outside Hong Kong rebounded after a slight decline in the first half. By currency, HKD loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half, while foreign currency loans recorded growth of 3.2% as Mainland borrowers gradually reduced their repayment of foreign currency loans. Banks' funding positions remained largely sound. The HKD loan-to-deposit ratio edged down to 77.1% at the end of 2016, reflecting deposit growth outpacing loan growth. The overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 59.9% at year-end, while the US dollar loan-to-deposit ratio dropped markedly to 63.8% due to strong growth in US dollar deposits. Owing to US dollar strength, both onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates weakened. Against this backdrop, Hong Kong's CNH liquidity pool (including customer deposits and certificate of deposit balances) consolidated further with other offshore renminbi markets, and the volatility of the CNH HIBOR increased significantly. Nevertheless, banks continued to manage their liquidity in renminbi soundly, and the average daily turnover of the RMB RTGS system remained at a high level. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business will likely continue to face headwinds arising from uncertainty over the renminbi exchange rate trajectory. As global market conditions improved, Hong Kong's stock market closed substantially higher during the reporting period. Although the US presidential election produced an unexpected result, the market was only briefly affected. This was mainly because investors were optimistic about the Trump administration's fiscal stimulus measures, which drove global equity markets higher. Although benefiting from this, the local market was cautious amid the optimism, possibly due to concerns over the accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes, challenges to Mainland China's economic outlook, uncertainty over renminbi policy, and controls on capital flows. Looking ahead, although the local market may be affected by external economic conditions, its attractive valuations could provide support to the market. Although HKD bond yields rose sharply late last year, and the spread against US Treasury bonds widened rapidly, the HKD bond market continued to expand steadily during the reporting period. Meanwhile, Hong Kong's CNH debt market recovered in the second half of the year after contracting in the first half of 2016, but new bond issuance recorded for the full year still declined from the previous year. Looking ahead, if global investors reverse their earlier yield-seeking investment strategies, both the HKD and CNH debt markets would come under pressure. As US trade policy remains unclear and the renminbi exchange rate may remain volatile, the outlook for these two bond markets over the next six months will continue to be beset by significant uncertainties. Following the government's introduction of the new stamp duty measures, the residential property market immediately showed signs of adjustment, but has recently rebounded. Given the renewed market exuberance, the government uniformly raised the stamp duty to 15% in November. Transaction volumes in both the primary and secondary markets declined over the following two months. However, transaction volumes have risen recently, partly reflecting an increase in developers' launches of primary market projects. At the same time, property prices continued to rise to new highs, though the pace of increase has slowed.

Following Trump's unexpected election as US President, uncertainty over US policy has increased accordingly. Although market attention has focused on the short-term benefits arising from the possible implementation of large-scale fiscal policy and business facilitation measures, US economic activity is now close to its economic potential, and fiscal stimulus measures may only bring a slight cyclical boost to US economic growth, while further intensifying the upside risk to inflation. More importantly, the risks faced by emerging market economies are rising along with the accelerating pace of US interest rate hikes and the fund outflow pressures brought about by a strengthening US dollar, while possible US trade protectionism measures will also threaten global trade flows. In East Asia, real economic activity improved slightly in the second half of 2016, and export volumes have recently increased. However, against the backdrop of US interest rate hikes, US dollar appreciation, and possible US protectionist measures, financial markets should continue to be volatile, and downside risks to economic growth are rising. In Mainland China, amid robust growth in infrastructure investment and improved private-sector business spending, overall economic growth accelerated slightly in the second half of 2016. The Mainland economy continued to rebalance, with the tertiary industry expanding steadily, but the continued advancement of economic restructuring and changes in Sino-US trade relations may increase uncertainty over the near-term economic outlook. With the government determined to curb rising home prices, if the housing market continues to cool, the real estate sector's contribution to economic growth this year may also diminish. On the external front, although the renminbi remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) basket of currencies during the reporting period, capital outflow pressures increased towards the end of 2016 as the US dollar appreciated and the US raised interest rates, and subsequently appeared to ease somewhat in early 2017. Following Trump's unexpected election as US President, global financial markets reacted strongly, particularly as markets anticipated that Trump's policies—such as tax reform, large-scale increases in infrastructure spending, and deregulation—would push up US economic growth and inflation, stimulating major equity markets to rise (Figure 2.1). As a result, market expectations of US inflation and US interest rate hikes heated up, causing yields on US Central Government bonds to surge and the US dollar to strengthen. Figure 2.1 Equity market indices of selected advanced economies. However, the tax-cut measures anticipated by the market from Trump may not produce the positive impact on US economic growth that the market expects. Although a shift in economic policy towards reliance on fiscal easing measures would help relieve the heavy burden borne by policy-easing, given the current stage of the US economic cycle, it is debatable whether now is the appropriate time to implement fiscal easing measures. Although US economic growth has slowed in recent quarters, the output gap is gradually narrowing, and the February unemployment rate was in line with the Fed's estimated natural unemployment rate of 4.7%, reflecting that US economic activity is already close to its economic potential. The US economy is currently in an expansionary cycle, and the fiscal multiplier would be lower than during a recession (see, for example, Auerbach and Gorodnichenko (2012))1. In fact, recent estimates of the US Laffer curve suggest that tax cuts on labour or capital may lead to reduced tax revenue (see, for example, Trabandt and Uhlig (2012))2. In any case, with excess capacity diminishing, any measure to further boost economic growth—even if its actual impact on economic growth is limited—may also push up inflation. At the same time, other factors such as rising oil and commodity prices, as well as potential trade protectionism measures including the Border Adjustment Tax now under consideration, may also intensify the upside risk to US inflation. Even as the risk of rising US inflation increases, the Fed has remained cautious about tightening US monetary policy and tends to maintain an ultra-accommodative monetary policy stance. However, long-term bond yields have risen, partly reflecting increased US inflation risk. Since the US election, although market forecasts for future federal funds rates have been revised up to close to the Fed's median projections for 2017 and early 2018, they remain far below the Fed's long-term projections (Figure 2.2). Therefore, an accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes may trigger the risk of sharp market volatility. Although financial markets have focused on the short-term benefits arising from the possible implementation of expansionary fiscal policy and business facilitation measures that would drive stronger US economic growth, long-term risks persist, including damaging protectionist trade policies and further rises in US Central Government bond yields. Indeed, the Trump administration may fulfil its campaign promises and adopt trade protectionism measures. Increased trade barriers would cause market distortions that harm overall interests, hamper global trade flows, reduce the efficiency of the global supply chain, and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. Figure 2.2 Future federal funds rate projections: Fed versus market. In Europe, political instability remains the main risk and headwind to Europe's economic recovery. Although the economic environment in the Euro area has gradually improved, with fourth-quarter real GDP growing moderately by 1.7% year-on-year, only slightly below the 1.8% year-on-year growth in the third quarter, compared with the stronger recovery of the US economy, economic activity in the Euro area remains only slightly above pre-global financial crisis levels (Figure 2.3). Since the UK's decision to leave the EU last summer, markets have been concerned that the Euro area may eventually disintegrate. Although Italy's economic and political situation appears to have stabilised after forming a new government and implementing measures to rescue the banking sector, against the backdrop of Brexit negotiations and rising anti-establishment sentiment, the upcoming elections in Germany and France (and possibly Italy) may become political flashpoints. Partly due to increased political uncertainty, sovereign yields in Europe have continued to climb, while corporate bonds spreads have also widened, a situation that is especially pronounced in peripheral countries, potentially creating a vicious cycle for the real economy and possibly placing pressure on real business investment in the Euro area. Figure 2.3 Real GDP of major advanced economies. In Japan, real GDP in recent quarters was revised upward, with the year-on-year growth rate in the fourth quarter of 2016 rising to 1.6%, the fastest pace since the third quarter of 2015, and the economic recovery was stronger than previously expected. However, partly due to structural problems in the labour market, wage growth has been slow, resulting in weak consumption growth. At the same time, the recent rapid depreciation of the yen means that the downward pressures on "new core" goods inflation caused by the earlier yen appreciation are about to begin to fade. Coupled with a stronger-than-expected recovery, this indicates that the near-term inflation outlook has improved, and "new core" inflation (excluding fresh food and energy), although falling to 0.1% in December, is expected to bottom out and rebound. Nevertheless, in the face of long-term and structural headwinds, growth may remain sluggish, and inflation expectations remain at around 0.5%–0.6%, below the level when Abenomics was launched in early 2014, so the risk that inflation fails to reach the Bank of Japan's 2% medium-term target still persists. For other countries, especially emerging market economies, since US imports have declined following the global financial crisis and the US may implement protectionist policies, the benefits brought by faster US economic growth through the trade channel may be smaller. Meanwhile, the accelerating pace of US interest rate hikes and further appreciation of the US dollar will lead to tighter financial conditions, exacerbating downside risks to the economy. This may drag down economic growth and increase the risk of rapid capital outflows. In fact, market expectations of large-scale fiscal expansion by the Trump administration, together with concerns about surging energy prices, have led to a repricing of inflation risk, causing long-term bond yields to rise significantly across the board in advanced economies as well as in many emerging market economies. Accelerated growth in private consumption and buoyant public-sector building and construction activities drove Hong Kong's economic growth to pick up slightly in the second half of 2016. With the external environment becoming increasingly uncertain, economic growth is expected to be moderate in 2017. Benefiting from stable import prices and moderate local growth drivers, inflationary pressures are expected to remain under control. Hong Kong's economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew by 1.2% quarter-on-quarter in the fourth quarter, slightly higher than the 0.8% growth rate in the third quarter (Chart 3.1). Partly due to improved consumer confidence and robust labour market conditions, private consumption grew at a faster pace, becoming the main driver of GDP growth. Supported by infrastructure projects such as the third runway at Hong Kong airport, building and construction activities also became buoyant. However, owing to weak corporate capital spending, the contribution of aggregate investment spending to GDP growth narrowed. On the external front, both merchandise exports and imports accelerated as intra-regional trade flows rose (Chart 3.2).22 Trade-related and transport services drove exports of services to grow further, while imports of services rebounded partly due to strong travel demand from local residents. Net exports continued to drag on GDP growth. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contributions of major expenditure components Chart 3.2 Real imports and exports The labour market remained tight. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate stayed at 3.4% in the first three quarters, before edging down to 3.3% in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.3). In fact, the unemployment rate in a number of major sectors declined in the second half of the year, including the retail, accommodation and food services sectors, partly because the slowdown in the retail sector had stabilised. Total employment reached a new high of 3.824 million in February 2017, while the labour force participation rate remained stable at around 61%. Chart 3.3 Unemployment rate and total employment Real economic growth is expected to remain moderate in 2017. On the external front, given the uncertainties in the global macroeconomic and financial conditions, global economic and trade growth may remain moderate. Coupled with the strong US dollar pushing up the real effective exchange rate index of the HKD, this will dampen Hong Kong's export performance. On the domestic front, although stable employment and income conditions will support consumption, private consumption is expected to grow moderately, dragged down by rising interest rates. With increased housing supply and the commencement of a number of infrastructure projects, building and construction activities should grow steadily, but subdued business sentiment and rising interest rates will restrain corporate capital spending. The Government currently forecasts real GDP growth of between 2% and 3% in 2017, while private-sector analysts forecast an average of 2.0%. The growth outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties, with those from the external environment being particularly significant. Policy uncertainty of the new US administration will cloud the global economic outlook, and possible trade protectionism policies would pose headwinds to global trade flows. The Brexit process and elections in several major European countries may also lead to volatility in asset markets and affect the flow of HKD funds. In addition, US interest rate normalisation will tighten local monetary conditions and pose downward pressures on the real economy and asset prices. Since the second half of 2016, although local inflation has picked up in quarter-on-quarter momentum in recent months, it has remained moderate overall. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index held steady at 2.1% from the second half of 2016 to January this year (Chart 3.4). The underlying inflation on a three-month-on-three-month annualised basis, which reflects inflation momentum, accelerated from 0.9% in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, before easing slightly to 2.4% in January. The pick-up in inflation momentum was mainly due to rising prices of traded goods and housing rental (Chart 3.5). In particular, inflation of traded goods prices rose from negative in the third quarter to 3.0% in the fourth quarter, driven mainly by basic food as well as clothing and footwear prices. At the same time, since the third quarter, as the decline in residential rentals narrowed and public housing rentals were raised in September 2016, the housing rental component of the composite consumer price index rose, but subsequently eased slightly in January (Chart 3.6). Chart 3.4 Different measures reflecting consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Consumer price inflation by major components Chart 3.6 Rental component of composite CPI and market rentals In the near term, owing to weak import prices and moderate domestic cost pressures, inflationary pressures are expected to remain under control. As the strong HKD partly offsets the impact of the rebound in global commodity prices, imported inflation will stay low (Chart 3.7). On the domestic front, the output gap was estimated to remain close to zero in the fourth quarter of 2016, which should help ease business cost pressures and thereby restrain inflation in the services components. Despite the tight labour market, wage increases in recent quarters have been mild, with real wage per person rising by 1.1% in the first half of 2016 before falling by 0.4% in the third quarter (Chart 3.8). Given the persistent uncertainties in the external environment leading to cautious business sentiment, the increase in labour cost should be restrained against this backdrop. In addition, owing to the weak retail sales performance in recent months, the increase in retail property rentals is expected to be moderate. Furthermore, the impact of the earlier softening in residential rentals will gradually emerge, which will also help ease inflationary pressures. Overall, the year-on-year inflation rate is expected to decline over the whole of 2017, with the Government forecasting a full-year underlying inflation of 2.0%, lower than the 2.3% in 2016. Chart 3.7 Commodity and import prices Chart 3.8 Unit labour cost and real wage per person The inflation outlook faces both upside and downside risks. In terms of downside risks, if inflation accelerates in the US under the Trump administration, this may prompt the US to raise interest rates faster than expected, which could push up local mortgage rates and increase downward pressures on property prices and housing rental. At the same time, the appreciation of the HKD may keep import prices weak and, at the same time, weaken the local appeal to visitor arrivals into Hong Kong. In terms of upside risk, if the global economic expansion is faster than expected, it may accelerate Hong Kong's economic growth and push up demand-driven international commodity prices, thereby posing upward pressure on local inflation. In addition, the revised statutory minimum wage will take effect on 1 May 2017, which may further push up inflation, but the actual impact of this cost-push inflation will depend on the extent to which wage costs are passed on to consumer prices.

Despite financial market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained broadly stable, while HKD interbank interest rates rose in tandem with their USD counterparts. Partly due to improvements in the local economic environment, overall loans continued to grow moderately. Looking ahead, HKD fund flows may become more volatile amid an accelerated pace of interest rate normalisation in the US, uncertainty over the policy direction of the new US administration, and political risks in Europe. Despite financial market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar remained broadly stable (Chart 4.1). Although the market volatility triggered by the US presidential election in November led to a broad-based decline in Asian currencies, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar remained steady. However, the interest rate projections released by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) at its meeting on 13–14 December 2016 fuelled market expectations of faster US interest rate hikes, causing the Hong Kong dollar to weaken briefly thereafter. In early 2017, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened along with other Asian currencies, but it began to show signs of weakening as market expectations of a US rate hike in March rose from mid-February. During the reporting period, the CUs were not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Exchange rate and fund flow indicators; Chart 4.2 Fund flow indicators. As the US dollar strengthened, the nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar rose 4.9% between August and December, before stabilising recently (Chart 4.3). As the impact of the narrowing inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was mild, the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar closely tracked the movement of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates. Portfolio investment recorded outflows in the second half of 2016. The latest balance of payments statistics showed that non-resident investment in equity and debt securities registered net inflows in the third quarter, reflecting improved global market sentiment and substantial IPO activities (Table 4.A). However, partly driven by Hong Kong banks increasing their holdings of US bonds, resident debt investment recorded sizeable outflows that outweighed the investment inflows from non-residents. As a result, cross-border portfolio investment recorded net outflows in the third quarter. A survey of global mutual funds showed that portfolio investment outflows occurred in the final quarter of 2016, mainly because of the unexpected US presidential election result, coupled with expectations of a faster pace of US rate hikes, which put pressure on the local financial market as well as other Asian markets (Chart 4.4). However, the latest data showed that Hong Kong's portfolio investment saw inflow pressure in the first quarter of 2017, partly due to investors' optimism over the US adopting an expansionary fiscal policy, which improved the performance of the global financial market. Chart 4.4 Market surveys of equity- and bond-related fund flows. Looking ahead, HKD fund flows may become more volatile. If the pace of US interest rate normalisation accelerates, this would increase the risk of a reversal in HKD fund flows. At the same time, fund flows may become more volatile amid uncertainties surrounding the new US administration, the Brexit process, and elections in EU member states. In addition, increased investment demand from Mainland investors for Hong Kong dollar assets may create inflow pressure for the Hong Kong dollar. Although northbound trading exceeded southbound trading in scale during the initial period following the launch of the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect in December, two-way equity investment fund flows between the Mainland and Hong Kong under this scheme are expected to increase gradually. Despite rising US dollar interest rates and financial market volatility, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2016 and in recent months. The HKD Monetary Base remained sizeable, rising a further 1.7% in the second half, driven by growth in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued notes and coins in circulation (Chart 4.5). As the CUs were not triggered, the sum of the Aggregate Balance and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes remained broadly at the high level of HK$1,222.7 billion. Of this, the Aggregate Balance contracted while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes rose correspondingly, owing to the additional issuance of HK$49 billion of Exchange Fund Bills to meet banks' strong demand to manage their liquidity. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base. As the local economy became more robust, the pace of HKD money supply growth quickened. Growth in Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (Hong Kong dollar M3) accelerated from 2.3% in the first half to 6.5% in the second half. As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits recorded faster growth of 6.6% in the second half (Chart 4.7), mainly driven by increased transaction demand amid stronger local economic activity and a rebound in IPO activities. Analysed by counterpart assets, the growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 mainly reflected increases in Hong Kong dollar loans and banks' net foreign currency assets (Chart 4.6), which respectively reflected money created by credit expansion and net inflows of HKD funds into the non-bank private sector. Chart 4.6 Changes in Hong Kong dollar M3 and its counterpart assets. On the other hand, growth in foreign currency deposits remained mixed. After rising 10.2% in the first half, US dollar deposits recorded a higher increase of 12.8% in the second half amid the strong US dollar (Chart 4.7). By contrast, other foreign currency deposits contracted a further 10.3%, mainly due to a decline in renminbi deposits. Overall, growth in the total deposits of AIs rose to 6.2% in the second half of 2016, with full-year growth at 9.1%. Chart 4.7 Deposit growth. Amid expectations of US interest rate normalisation, banks' wholesale cost of funding rose in the fourth quarter of 2016. Although HKD interbank interest rates remained low, they rose partly driven by year-end financing needs and by catching up with the increase in their USD counterparts. Overnight and three-month HIBORs rose 54 and 46 basis points respectively in the second half to 0.66% and 1.02% (Chart 4.8). Global financial markets experienced renewed volatility at the beginning of the year as markets reassessed inflation risks in the United States. In February, global equity markets fell sharply from their late-January highs, completely offsetting the significant gains recorded at the start of the year, while the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. Over the past two years, global equity markets rose persistently amid low volatility, as markets expected the economic environment to continue its solid growth while inflation and interest rates remained at ideally low levels. However, this expectation now faces the risks of tightening global monetary conditions, rising trade protectionism sentiment, and heightened geopolitical tensions. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, while markets continued to function in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, overall loans continued to increase, but at a slower pace. After a modest slowdown in the middle of last year, both property price gains and transaction volumes rebounded in the fourth quarter of 2017. Looking ahead, the re-emergence of volatility in global and local financial markets may add to the volatility of fund flows in Hong Kong. Given the uncertainties in financial markets, as well as the ongoing normalisation of US monetary policy and persistent geopolitical risks, banks should remain vigilant against increased interest rate volatility and potential capital outflow risks. In particular, given the continued rise in corporate leverage levels and the elevated household debt burden, banks should assess the potential impact on asset quality should interest rates rise more than expected. Following a period of over two years during which the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) hovered at low levels, global financial markets experienced renewed volatility at the beginning of the year. Global equity markets fell sharply from their late-January highs, with the S&P 500 Index dropping by more than 10% at one point, completely offsetting the significant gains recorded in early January. Market sentiment shifted, as signs emerged that the global economic recovery could exert pressure on the long-subdued US wages and prices, potentially prompting the US Federal Reserve to accelerate its pace of rate hikes. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also rose to a four-year high. The prolonged rise in global equity markets over the past two years was built on market expectations that economic conditions would remain favourable. In the second half of 2017, the momentum of global economic growth continued to strengthen, with economic activity in both advanced economies and emerging market economies picking up in tandem. Towards the end of the year, the US Congress passed a tax reform package, which included tax cuts and a comprehensive overhaul of corporate and personal tax rules, leading markets to anticipate that the strong US economic recovery would receive additional cyclical stimulus in the near term. Despite the strengthening of activity, core inflation in major advanced economies remained moderate, further reinforcing market expectations that global interest rates would remain low for an extended period. Against this backdrop, global asset markets rose significantly in 2017, with US equity markets in particular repeatedly reaching new highs. However, following the release of stronger-than-expected US wage growth data for January, global equity markets reassessed inflation risks. After the short-term financial market volatility, the risk of tightening global monetary conditions may continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. In the United States, the economy has now reached its output potential, and the cyclical stimulus of tax cuts to domestic demand is expected to accelerate the rebound in inflation, thereby prompting the US Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy at a faster pace. At the same time, as tax cuts lead to a rising fiscal deficit, the United States may issue more Treasury bonds in the future, which is expected to add upward pressure on long-term bond yields as the US Federal Reserve continues to advance the normalisation of its balance sheet. Outside the United States, the strengthening growth momentum in other major advanced economies has led markets to expect that their central banks may scale back the size of their quantitative easing programmes. If implemented, this would lead to a synchronised tightening of global monetary conditions. Policy and event risks arising from international political and geopolitical tensions may also cast a shadow over the outlook for global economic growth. The US government appears increasingly inclined to adopt trade protectionism measures to protect domestic industries from competition, with recent examples including the announcement of import tariffs on solar panels, washing machines, steel, and aluminium. These moves have raised concerns about whether its trading partners will respond with retaliatory measures. In addition, should geopolitical tensions escalate unexpectedly, global trade could be affected, and financial market volatilities could intensify. Given the above uncertainties in the global economic outlook, whether the currently elevated valuations of global asset markets can be sustained remains in question. From a fundamental perspective, it remains to be seen whether the cyclical increase in global demand and the rising fiscal deficit arising from expected US tax cuts will push up the natural rate of interest (R*); moreover, the normalisation of the US Federal Reserve's balance sheet is expected to lead to a rise in the term premium, which may push up long-term interest rates, thereby weighing on asset market valuations. In East Asia, regional economies were also in an ideal environment of solid growth and moderate inflation. Amid strong economic performance and an optimistic outlook, capital inflows also accelerated, and financial markets rose in tandem. However, this favourable outlook faces downside risks from various factors: the synchronised advancement of monetary policy normalisation by major central banks tightening global liquidity; the US government's inward-looking trade policies; heightened geopolitical tensions; and the potential tightening of offshore US dollar liquidity as US corporations repatriate profits on a large scale in response to the one-off "deemed repatriation" provision under the country's tax reform. Should credit and financial markets face any shock, this could trigger a reversal of fund flows, and industries and economies with higher leverage levels are most vulnerable to the impact of tightening financial conditions. In Mainland China, the economy performed well in the second half of 2017, supported by factors such as robust consumption, strong infrastructure, and a rebound in industrial spending towards the end of the year. Meanwhile, signs of the rise of the "new economy" have become increasingly evident, as sectors such as high value-added manufacturing and services demonstrated strong business expansion momentum over the past few quarters. Looking ahead, the near-term growth outlook remains positive, though uncertainties persist. In particular, it remains to be seen to what extent the rapid growth of the "new economy" can help offset the short-term pressure on growth from the further advancement of structural reforms. The Mainland authorities announced in 2018 that they would continue to adopt a proactive fiscal policy stance, which may help cushion adverse economic developments when necessary. During the review period, some progress was made in both structural reforms and the control of systemic risks. In particular, with the introduction of tightening measures, the Mainland housing market showed signs of cooling during the review period, most notably in first-tier cities. At the same time, as banks tightened their loan approval standards, banks' risk exposures to enterprises in industries with excess capacity remained under control, while shadow banking activity also slowed amid financial deleveraging. In addition to the above positive developments, our analysis also suggests that the efficiency of capital allocation in Mainland China appears to have improved. In particular, the borrowing constraints faced by state-owned enterprises (SOEs) with weaker repayment capacity appear to have tightened, possibly due to a reduction in the support provided by local governments (for details, please refer to Box 2 on page 28). On the external front, amid a stabilising economic situation and diminishing risks, capital outflow pressure remained moderate for most of 2017. The Hong Kong economy maintained its sequential growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Real GDP grew by 3.8% for the full year of 2017, the fastest pace in nearly six years. Owing to favourable employment and income conditions as well as rising asset prices, private consumption continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2017. Aggregate investment spending also rebounded on the back of increased corporate capital expenditure. On the external front, benefiting from improved global trade growth and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism, Hong Kong's export performance improved further. Nevertheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net exports of goods continued to drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution to GDP growth. Economic growth is expected to remain solid in 2018, with private consumption, building and construction activities, and exports continuing to support economic growth. Given that HKD interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. The Government's and market consensus forecasts for real GDP growth in 2018 are in the range of 3 to 4% and 3.0% respectively. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook remains affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned above, the economic performance of Mainland China amid tightening financial conditions, and the movements of Hong Kong's asset markets. Although the unemployment rate fell to 2.9%, a nearly 20-year low, local inflationary pressure remained contained. Nevertheless, there have been signs of a slight rise in sequential inflation momentum in recent months, with the prices of both tradable goods and services rising. Looking ahead, the underlying inflation rate may edge up to a still-moderate level, partly reflecting the pass-through effect of rising fresh-letting private residential rentals. The global economy's synchronised strengthening momentum since late 2016 has shown no signs of weakening. Improving growth outlook drove global stock markets steadily higher through 2017 and into early 2018. However, as markets reassessed US inflation risks, global stock markets experienced a sell-off and sharp volatility in February, marking an end to the two years of calm in financial markets. Looking ahead, the risk of tightening global financing conditions, along with a range of policy and event risks, will continue to cast a shadow over the global growth outlook. Against a tight labour market, US tax cuts could accelerate a cyclical rebound in inflation, prompting the Fed to speed up the pace of monetary policy tightening. As the Fed continues to advance balance sheet normalisation, increased issuance of US Central Government bonds to fund the tax cuts could add to the upside risk on long-term US Treasury bond yields. The spectre of rising trade barriers, along with any unexpected escalation in geopolitical tensions, could also threaten the nascent global trade recovery. In East Asia, benefiting from strong export performance and stable domestic demand, real GDP growth continued to rise in the second half of 2017. However, while the economic outlook is optimistic, it also faces various downside risks, such as a potentially greater-than-expected tightening of global monetary conditions, US inward-looking trade policies, and geopolitical tensions. Should these downside risks materialise, they would also heighten the risk of a reversal in capital flows. Policymakers face multiple challenges: on the one hand, guarding against risks to economic growth, and on the other, limiting the impact of prolonged accommodative financing conditions on inflation and balance sheet vulnerabilities. In Mainland China, the economy performed well in the second half of 2017. During the review period, some progress was made in structural reforms and in containing systemic risks. The near-term growth outlook remains positive, but uncertainties persist, partly depending on the extent to which the rapid expansion of the "new economy" can offset the short-term pressures on growth arising from further advancing structural reforms. As economic conditions stabilised and risks eased, capital outflow pressures remained moderate for most of 2017. As the momentum of cyclical economic improvement has grown more firmly entrenched since late 2016, growth in advanced economies and emerging market economies accelerated in tandem in 2017. Among the major advanced economies, the United States saw robust growth in investment and exports, driven by optimistic private-sector sentiment and a sharp depreciation of the US dollar, while the Euro area and Japan also recorded broad-based cyclical recoveries. Exports of emerging market economies also benefited from the stabilisation of global commodity prices and increased import demand from major advanced economies. In the short term, following the passage of US tax reform, investment and consumption are expected to be further boosted by reductions in corporate and personal income taxes. In view of the current cyclical economic upswing and the expansionary effects of US tax reform, the International Monetary Fund forecast in January that global economic growth would accelerate from an estimated 3.7% in 2017 to 3.9% in 2018 (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real GDP growth forecasts As growth momentum in the Euro area and Japan strengthened, markets anticipated a narrowing of global monetary policy divergence, which, coupled with a more optimistic global growth outlook, spurred increased risk appetite and capital inflows into emerging market economies, thereby putting pressure on the US dollar. Despite the Fed raising interest rates three times during the year and beginning to advance balance sheet normalisation, the US dollar index still recorded a decline of nearly 10% in 2017. Meanwhile, despite broad-based acceleration in economic growth, core inflation in major advanced economies remained subdued and below their central banks' targets, leading markets until recently to expect that global interest rates would remain low (Chart 2.2). Against this backdrop, global stock markets rose steadily through 2017 and into early 2018, with the S&P 500 index repeatedly hitting record highs, pushing the cyclically-adjusted price-to-earnings ratio up to 33.8 in January 2018, the highest level since the "dot-com bubble" in early 2000. Chart 2.2 Core inflation in major advanced economies However, since the second half of 2017, market concerns that tax cuts would lead to a rising budget deficit and inflation have driven US long-term US Treasury bond yields steadily higher, casting doubt on the sustainability of increasingly elevated asset market valuations. As the US reported higher-than-expected average hourly wage growth for January 2018, markets reassessed US inflation risks, triggering a correction in global stock markets in early February 2018. The S&P 500 index at one point fell more than 10% from its high on 26 January, fully offsetting the significant gains at the start of the year, and remained under pressure after the US government announced a new round of trade protection measures in early March. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield also climbed to a four-year high in mid-February. Market volatility rose sharply, with the Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index at one point spiking to a two-year high of 37.3, marking the end of the persistent narrow-range environment of the past two years (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index (VIX) Looking ahead, after the short-term stock market volatility, US inflation risks, the upside risk on long-term US Treasury bond yields, and possible monetary policy tightening by other major central banks could all lead to a tightening of global monetary conditions, thereby casting a shadow over the global economic growth outlook. First, with regard to US inflation risks, the recently passed tax reform includes several provisions expected to provide a short-term cyclical stimulus to private consumption and investment. The key measures involved in the tax reform include: (1) lowering corporate and personal income tax rates, (2) temporarily allowing full expensing of capital investment, and (3) a one-off "deemed repatriation" provision that helps reduce the incentive for US firms to park their overseas earnings abroad. While it remains uncertain how the tax cuts will affect domestic demand and inflation, with the US economy now having reached its output potential, the tax cuts could push US output beyond its potential, thereby leading to economic overheating and a cyclical rebound in inflation. Should inflationary pressures rise more than expected, this could prompt the Fed to accelerate the pace of monetary policy tightening. Currently, the federal funds rate trajectory anticipated by financial markets is more gradual than the projections released by the Fed. However, should inflation rebound unexpectedly, the risk of an abrupt repricing of rate hike expectations cannot be ruled out (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Federal funds rate projections Second, given that the tax reform could aggravate the budget deficit, issuance of US Central Government bonds is expected to increase going forward. As the Fed continues to advance its balance sheet normalisation programme, this is expected to lead to a rise in the term premium; under such circumstances, increased issuance of US Central Government bonds could intensify the upward pressure on long-term US Treasury bond yields. Furthermore, as markets increasingly anticipated the likelihood of the US passing the tax cut package, US inflation expectations have risen steadily since the second half of 2017 (Chart 2.5). As a result, after hovering at low levels for most of 2017, the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield has risen by more than 70 basis points since the third quarter, partly reflecting market concerns over increased bond supply pressures and rising inflation expectations. Chart 2.5 5-year 5-year forward inflation expectations In addition, a key question is whether the natural rate of interest (R\*), a major component of long-term interest rates, will remain low over the long term as most expect. While estimates of R\* vary, it is widely believed to have fallen substantially since the global financial crisis (Chart 2.6). Nonetheless, owing to (1) an expected decline in the national savings rate as the budget deficit increases, and (2) the potential for a higher investment rate due to corporate tax cuts and more favourable tax treatment of capital expenditure, the US R\* may face upside risk in the future. Amid buoyant domestic demand and improved export performance, the Hong Kong economy maintained solid growth drivers in the second half of 2017. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. The economic outlook for Hong Kong remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the normalisation of monetary policy by major central banks, the stability of global financial markets, rising protectionist sentiment, and escalating geopolitical tensions. In the short term, although domestic inflationary pressures should remain moderate, certain upside risks still persist. The Hong Kong economy maintained its growth drivers in the second half of 2017. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew by 0.8% quarter-on-quarter in both the third and fourth quarters, comparable to the average growth rate of 0.9% in the preceding two quarters (Chart 3.1). Compared with the first half of the year, private consumption continued to grow solidly and remained one of the main drivers of GDP growth. The solid consumption growth was attributable to favourable employment and income conditions, still-optimistic consumer sentiment, and the positive impact of rising asset prices through the wealth effect. Although building and construction activities weakened, increased corporate capital spending caused aggregate investment spending to rise markedly in the final quarter, after having been broadly stable for three quarters. On the external front, benefiting from improved global trade growth and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism, Hong Kong's export performance improved further (Chart 3.2). Nonetheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net exports of goods continued to drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution to GDP growth. Chart 3.1 real GDP growth rate and contributions by major expenditure component. Chart 3.2 Real imports and exports. Sustained economic growth drivers boosted employment in the second half of 2017. During the period, total employment increased by about 0.7% to over 3.85 million persons, with the construction sector, the financing and business services sector, as well as the public administration, social and personal services sector recording the most notable gains. As real GDP growth outpaced employment growth, labour productivity showed signs of further improvement. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance will continue to benefit from the improved global economic growth outlook and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism. On the domestic front, private consumption is expected to continue to grow, mainly due to favourable labour market conditions. Given that HKD interest rates will eventually rise, Box 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. As for domestic fixed capital formation, benefiting from increased housing supply and the ongoing launch of infrastructure projects, building and construction activities should grow steadily. Although the improved economic environment will stimulate business capital spending, potential interest rate hikes may have a negative impact. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of between 3% and 4% in 2018, while growth forecasts by international organisations and private sector analysts range between 2% and 4%. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned in the preceding sections, the economic performance of Mainland China amid tightening financial conditions, and the movements of Hong Kong's asset markets. Domestic inflationary pressures remained contained in the second half of 2017, but the sequential inflation momentum showed signs of a slight pick-up in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index rose by 1.7% and 1.6% in the third and fourth quarters respectively, comparable to the average increase of about 1.7% in the first half of the year. However, the three-month-on-three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, edged up to 2.8% in January 2018 (Chart 3.3). Prices of both traded goods and services rose. The rebound in fresh-letting private residential rentals since mid-2016 may also have added, to some extent, to inflation momentum (Chart 3.4). In addition, labour cost pressures remained moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Different indicators reflecting consumer price inflation. Chart 3.4 Composite consumer price index rental component and market rentals. Chart 3.5 unit labour cost and per capita salary. As global inflation remains moderate and domestic cost increases are stable, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong are expected to remain moderate in 2018, though the underlying inflation rate may gradually rebound from its eight-year low of 1.7% in 2017. For instance, owing to the pass-through effect of the growth in fresh-letting private residential rentals, inflationary pressures may increase somewhat in the second half of 2018. Market consensus forecasts put the headline inflation rate at a moderate 2.2% in 2018, while the Government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5%. Although the inflation outlook is moderate, upside risks still persist. On the external front, should global inflation or commodity prices record larger-than-expected increases, this could add to domestic inflation momentum. On the domestic front, the labour market has tightened further recently, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, marking the first time in nearly 20 years it fell below 3% (Chart 3.6). The current output gap is estimated to be close to zero, and a substantial further tightening of the labour market could pose additional upside pressure on inflation. Chart 3.6 unemployment rate. Amid the low interest rate environment following the 2008 global financial crisis, the mortgage debt of Hong Kong households increased. As the normalisation of USD interest rates proceeds, HKD interest rates will eventually rise in line with their USD counterparts, and household mortgage repayment burdens will correspondingly increase in the future, thereby dragging on household consumption. Therefore, this Box examines the impact of increased mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption in Hong Kong. The mortgage repayment burden refers to the ratio of mortgage debt servicing payments (i.e. interest payments plus loan principal amortisation) to income. Chart B3.1 illustrates the role of the mortgage repayment burden in the transmission of interest rate shocks to private consumption. In addition to the substitution effect, income effect, and the wealth effect and collateral effect arising from changes in asset prices as mentioned in general economic theory, in the presence of a mortgage repayment burden, an interest rate shock also affects private consumption by altering mortgage interest payment amounts and thereby changing households' disposable income. This impact will expand as the outstanding mortgage loan amount increases. In addition, the loan principal amortisation amount will change with variations in the outstanding mortgage loan amount, which also affects private consumption by altering households' disposable income. Chart B3.1 Determinants of private consumption. To measure the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption, we estimate the outstanding mortgage debt servicing ratio (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage debt. Unlike the current mortgage repayment burden indicator, which applies only to newly originated mortgage debt, the OMDSR covers all outstanding mortgage debt of the overall household sector, which is more closely related to total private consumption. Following broadly the methodology used by the Bank for International Settlements, we measure the OMDSR using the standard formula for fixed instalment payments: where Dt is the outstanding residential mortgage loan amount of the banking sector, Yt is the total income of owner-occupier households (indicated by the median income of owner-occupier households multiplied by the number of owner-occupier households), and rt and st are the average interest rate and maturity of outstanding mortgage loans respectively. To assess whether the OMDSR can reliably measure the mortgage repayment burden of the entire household sector, it is useful to compare the OMDSR with two commonly used repayment burden indicators. Chart B3.2 shows the estimated OMDSR from 1985 to mid-2017, as well as the median mortgage payment and loan repayment to income ratio estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on the quinquennial population census. In the early 2000s, both ratios exhibited a downward trend, consistent with the reduction in overall household mortgage borrowing following the bursting of the 1997 property bubble and the sharp decline in mortgage rates over the same period. Despite the substantial rise in property prices after the global financial crisis, both ratios remained stable, owing to the macro-prudential measures adopted by the HKMA on banks' mortgage lending, which curbed overall household mortgage leverage. In addition, the lengthening of the maturity of newly originated mortgage loans also reduced the actual amount of mortgage payments. Chart B3.2 OMDSR and the median mortgage payment and loan repayment to income ratio. We also compare the OMDSR with banks' debt servicing ratio, the latter being the actual debt servicing to income ratio of banks' new mortgage applicants. As shown in Chart B3.3, the OMDSR is lower than banks' debt servicing ratio, partly because the OMDSR covers not only new mortgages but also existing mortgages. As existing mortgages were taken out when housing prices were lower, their repayments are correspondingly lower than those of new mortgages. Therefore, the outstanding mortgage repayment burden indicator covering both existing and new mortgages (i.e. the OMDSR) is lower than the repayment burden indicator for new mortgages (i.e. banks' debt servicing ratio). In addition, banks' debt servicing ratio is higher partly because banks, in complying with the HKMA's prudential regulatory requirement, take non-mortgage loan repayments into account when calculating the debt servicing ratio. After the global financial crisis, both the OMDSR and banks' debt servicing ratio remained stable, mainly owing to the HKMA's implementation of prudential regulation on mortgage lending, which set a cap on banks' debt servicing ratio, a measure that also helped stabilise the OMDSR. Chart B3.3 OMDSR and banks' new mortgage debt servicing ratio. Overall, the OMDSR is broadly consistent with commonly used repayment burden indicators, but the OMDSR is more timely and can reflect the burden of overall outstanding mortgage debt, rather than only that of newly originated mortgage debt. Therefore, we believe the OMDSR can be used to assess the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption. To assess the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption in Hong Kong, we follow the methodology of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016) to estimate an error-correction model. In it, the long-run relationship between real private consumption (indicated by real average private consumption per household) and its determinants is represented in the short-run equation by an error-correction term. Based on existing theory and empirical evidence, we take real income (indicated by median household income, deflated by the composite consumer price index), real housing and financial wealth (indicated respectively by residential property prices and the Hang Seng Index, deflated by the composite consumer price index), and the OMDSR as the long-run determinants of private consumption.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, while the local interbank market continued to function in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, total lending continued to increase, but at a slower pace than in the first half. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalise, HKD interest rates may face greater upward pressures. Should global financial market sentiment change abruptly, the volatility of fund flows may increase. In the second half of 2017, the HKD-USD spot exchange rate moved between 7.799 and 7.827 (Chart 4.1). The HKD spot exchange rate briefly strengthened and held at around 7.80 during September to November 2017. This was mainly attributable to increased demand for funds from IPO fund-raising activities and the cautious attitude of banks in managing their liquidity ahead of month-ends and the year-end, which led to tighter liquidity conditions, in turn slowing interest rate arbitrage activities and increasing the unwinding of HKD short positions. As the tight HKD liquidity conditions eased and US dollar commercial demand rose ahead of the year-end, the HKD spot exchange rate softened again in mid-December 2017. Entering 2018, despite increased volatility in global financial markets (particularly the equity markets), the Hong Kong dollar continued to function in an orderly manner. During the reporting period, the HKD-USD exchange rate weakened, but the CUs were not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate. Chart 4.2 Fund flow indicators. The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar fluctuated slightly in the second half of 2017, but recently faced greater downward pressures as the US dollar weakened further (Chart 4.3). This was broadly in line with the movement of the US dollar against most major currencies. As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was very small and had limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index, the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar continued to closely track the movements of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates. Portfolio investment by non-residents recorded inflows in the second half of 2017. The latest balance of payments statistics showed that both resident and non-resident equity securities investment recorded inflows in the third quarter, reflecting an improved regional economic outlook and optimistic market sentiment (Table 4.A). Non-resident debt securities investment recorded inflows in the third quarter of 2017, offsetting the outflows of resident debt investment. A survey of global mutual funds also showed that both equity and debt investment recorded inflows in the fourth quarter of 2017, as the market held an optimistic attitude towards the economic outlook and firms’ earnings. In recent weeks, the survey data showed that despite corrections in global financial markets, equity investment still recorded inflows, while bond investment recorded slight outflows (Chart 4.4). Chart 4.4 Market survey of equity- and bond-related fund flows. Looking ahead, as the US monetary policy normalisation process continues, the negative interest rate spread between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar will widen, which may induce increased arbitrage activities. At the same time, given that the pace of US monetary policy normalisation remains uncertain, and global macro-financial conditions and market sentiment are ever-changing, the volatility of HKD funds flows and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may increase. The HKMA will continue to safeguard the stability of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate in accordance with the Currency Board mechanism with its full efforts. Despite the US Federal Reserve raising interest rates and continuing to shrink its balance sheet, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2017 and recently. In the second half of 2017, the HKD Monetary Base rose further by 1.4%, mainly driven by growth in the Certificates of Indebtedness issued for banknotes issuance (Chart 4.5). As the CUs were not triggered, the sum of the Aggregate Balance and the outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes remained largely unchanged in the second half, standing at around HK$1,226.8 billion. Of this, the Aggregate Balance shrank, while the outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes correspondingly increased. This was due to the additional issuance of Exchange Fund Bills (totalling HK$80 billion) to meet banks' strong demand in managing their liquidity. Entering 2018, despite the correction in the stock market, the Monetary Base remained stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base. Meanwhile, the HKD money supply grew further in the second half of 2017, but at a slower pace. The growth of the Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (HKD M3) slowed from 8.9% in the first half to 2.5% in the second half. As a major component of HKD M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits edged up 2.2% in the second half (Chart 4.7). Of this, demand deposits grew relatively fast in the second half, partly due to buoyant asset markets and rising investment demand. Analysis of the counterpart assets showed that the growth of HKD M3 was, on the one hand, supported by the strong growth of HKD loans (Chart 4.6), and, on the other hand, dragged down by the net outflow of HKD funds from the non-bank private sector and the contraction of banks' net foreign currency assets. By contrast, other foreign currency deposits rebounded significantly in the second half, rising by 8.4%, after declining continuously for more than two years. This was mainly driven by the recent rebound in renminbi deposits. As the growth of Hong Kong dollar deposits and US dollar deposits slowed, total deposits of AIs increased slightly by 3.0% in the second half, compared with a growth rate of 5.6% in the first half. During September to December 2017, demand for funds from IPO fund-raising activities rose, while banks adopted a cautious attitude towards managing their liquidity ahead of month-ends and the year-end, which put upward pressure on HKD interbank interest rates (Chart 4.8). Compared with six months earlier, the overnight and three-month HIBORs rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively, climbing to 0.25% and 1.26% respectively in December (in terms of monthly average). The negative interest rate spread between the one-month to three-month HKD and USD interbank interest rates also narrowed correspondingly. Chart 4.8 HKD and USD interbank interest rates. Meanwhile, the HKD yield curve shifted upward but flattened, broadly similar to the movement of the USD yield curve. In the second half, the yield of the three-year Hong Kong Government Bond rose by 63 basis points, closing at 1.52% at the end of 2017, while the yield of the ten-year Hong Kong Government Bond rose by a smaller extent of 33 basis points, closing at 1.83% at the end of 2017 (Chart 4.9). The overnight and three-month HIBORs closed at 0.43% and 1.08% respectively at the end of February 2018. At the retail level, although banks' lending rates rose along with the surge in HIBORs, banks' cost of funding generally remained low as the deposit base was still large. Despite intense competition in the mortgage lending business, banks' average lending rate for new mortgages gradually rose by 36 basis points to 2.16% in December (Chart 4.9), broadly following the upward trend of the one-month HIBOR. On the other hand, the composite interest rate, which measures the HKD cost of funding of retail banks, though briefly rose in October due to increased demand for funds from IPO fund-raising activities, remained soft for most of the second half, closing at 0.38% at the end of December. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalise and other major economies may begin interest rate normalisation, HKD interest rates may face greater upward pressure. At the same time, with fluctuating global market sentiment and ever-changing macro-financial conditions, the volatility of fund flows may increase. Nonetheless, the large HKD Monetary Base can serve as a buffer, helping to moderate an overly rapid rise in HKD interest rates. In addition, banks' prudent liquidity management and the ability to obtain discounts through the Discount Window also help contain excessive volatility in interbank interest rates. Bank credit grew strongly throughout 2017. The loan growth rate reached as high as 10.2% in the first half, slowing to 5.3% in the second half (Chart 4.10). By currency, given the favourable local economic environment and relatively low HKD cost of funding, HKD loans continued to grow rapidly by 9.5% in the second half, while foreign currency loans edged up only 0.1%. Retail banks' profitability improved in the second half of 2017 compared with the same period in 2016, mainly benefiting from the growth in net interest income. Capital and liquidity conditions remained robust. After experiencing strong loan growth in the first half of 2017, loan growth slowed in the second half, while asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Despite the notable rise in HKD interbank interest rates, retail banks' cost of HKD funds remained low due to the low retail deposit rates. This LTV ratio was well below the 64% recorded before the HKMA implemented the first round of countercyclical macroprudential measures (i.e. September 2009).

In the second half of 2018, the global economy continued to grow. However, while the US economy grew steadily, growth momentum in other regions slowed. Among advanced economies, growth in Japan and several major euro-area countries decelerated, with inflation remaining low. The slowdown in global trade flows and a significant drop in oil prices both posed cyclical headwinds to emerging market economies. In view of the slowing global growth momentum, the International Monetary Fund lowered its global growth forecasts for 2019 and 2020 in January by 0.2 and 0.1 percentage points respectively compared with its October 2018 forecasts. Due to a dimming growth outlook and escalating trade tensions, global equity markets fluctuated sharply at the end of 2018. The US Central Government bond yields curve flattened to levels not seen since the global financial crisis, sparking market concerns about an imminent US recession. However, US economic fundamentals remained solid, and the likelihood of a recession in the near term was low. Nonetheless, the global economic outlook remained fraught with uncertainties. In the US, while moderate inflation gave the Federal Reserve room to pause rate hikes, the Fed's data-dependent policy stance also signalled that financial markets may become more sensitive to data released going forward, particularly data that could prompt a tightening of monetary policy, such as a rise in US inflation.
