During the review period, the global economy continued to expand, but growth momentum weakened under the combined influence of idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds, particularly notable in regions outside the US. In view of the dimming growth outlook, the Fed adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasising that its decisions would be "data-dependent" and that "patience" was warranted, and no longer provided forward guidance on further interest rate hikes. As the Fed's policy inclination became data-dependent, financial markets may become more sensitive to data releases going forward, and may perceive monetary policy as more uncertain. Meanwhile, global trade policy uncertainties and heightened geopolitical risks may continue to cast a shadow over the global growth outlook. In East Asia, as the US rate hike cycle showed signs of moderating and the US dollar stabilised, financial markets have been broadly stable since the end of 2018. However, as the external environment deteriorated—namely the unresolved China-US trade conflict and weakening growth in advanced economies—the region may face a broad-based slowdown. In Mainland China, growth momentum slowed further in the second half of 2018, and amid the China-US trade conflict and financing difficulties faced by small enterprises, uncertainties surrounding the growth outlook increased. As a result, policymakers adopted more targeted measures to stabilise the economy and support private and small enterprises. Faced with these challenges, policymakers will need to strike a careful balance between continuing to prevent and control systemic risks and supporting enterprises and the real economy.  In the second half of 2018, the global economy continued to expand broadly. However, while the US economy's performance remained generally robust, some signs of slowing had emerged. There were also clear signs that growth momentum outside the US had moderated. A number of country-specific shocks—including natural disasters in Japan, the implementation of new automobile emission standards in Germany, the sharp rise in Italian Central Government bond yields due to the fiscal stand-off with the EU, and social unrest in France—all weighed on economic activity in advanced economies (Chart 2.1). In addition, a cyclical slowdown in global import growth constituted a headwind for industrial production in emerging market economies (Chart 2.2). The sharp drop in oil prices in the fourth quarter also posed new challenges for emerging market economies that export commodities. In view of the weakening growth momentum in the second half of 2018, the International Monetary Fund lowered its 2019 global growth forecast by 0.2 percentage points to 3.5% in January. Chart 2.1 Composite Purchasing Managers' Indices of selected advanced economies. Chart 2.2 Global import volume and industrial production of emerging market economies.  In the fourth quarter, global equity markets underwent a substantial correction, driven by the slowing global growth momentum, heightened trade policy uncertainties, market concerns over the sustainability of US firms' earnings growth, and the Fed's remarks that monetary policy would continue to tighten. As market sentiment in financial markets deteriorated, the US Central Government bond yields curve flattened to a level not seen since the global financial crisis, prompting some market participants to worry that a US recession was imminent (Chart 2.3). Chart 2.3 The yield spread between 10-year and 3-month US Central Government bond yields and the probability of a US recession. Nevertheless, the probability of a US recession in the near term is very low. US economic fundamentals remained sound, and in particular the tight labour market is expected to continue to support private consumption. At the same time, the US output gap is estimated to have only turned positive last year, making it less likely that overheating would prompt the Fed to tighten monetary policy substantially. However, possibly taking into account the substantial tightening of financial conditions since the fourth quarter, senior Fed officials began to emphasise in early January that monetary policy would be data-dependent, noting that mild inflationary pressures allowed them to be "patient" in determining future monetary policy adjustments. In addition, following its meeting in January, the Federal Open Market Committee no longer provided forward guidance on further interest rate hikes and announced that it "would be prepared to adjust any of the details for completing balance sheet normalisation in light of economic and financial developments". This shift triggered a rebound in global equity markets (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 S&P 500, MSCI World (excluding US) Index and MSCI Emerging Markets Index.  Despite the Fed's recent dovish pivot signals, the outlook for US monetary policy remains quite uncertain, depending on inflation and other developments. So far inflationary pressures have been mild, giving the Fed room to advance monetary normalisation gradually. Inflation expectations have remained stable in recent years, supporting the view that it "can be patient" (Chart 2.5). In addition, as Fed Chairman Powell pointed out in January, the US economic outlook faces multiple headwinds, including slowing growth outside the US and trade policy uncertainties. In view of these developments, the Fed may need to adopt a more cautious monetary policy stance. Chart 2.5 Market-based and survey-based measures of US inflation expectations. However, the tight labour market is expected to continue to support the US economy's overall performance. In this environment, wage growth may accelerate, which typically implies that future inflation may pick up (Chart 2.6). Therefore, the market's expectation, which has essentially ruled out the possibility of a Fed interest rate hike in 2019, may be overly optimistic (Chart 2.7). Chart 2.6 Average hourly earnings and core PCE inflation. Chart 2.7 Futures-implied probabilities of the federal funds target rate range remaining unchanged in 2019 versus at least one hike.  In sum, a prolonged pause in the Fed's rate hikes is by no means certain. To reduce policy errors, the Fed has increasingly emphasised that its decisions would be data-dependent, as a risk management strategy. It follows from this that financial markets may become more sensitive to data releases going forward, especially data that could prompt monetary policy tightening. The monetary policy of other major central banks is also uncertain. In the Euro area, the ECB terminated its asset purchase programme in December while continuing to reinvest in full the principal of maturing securities under the asset purchase programme, and reiterated its forward guidance of keeping the policy rate unchanged at least until the summer of 2019. However, in January the ECB lowered its short-term growth assessment, describing the risks to the growth outlook as having "moved to the downside". The implications of this downgrade of the ECB's economic growth assessment for monetary policy remain to be seen. In Japan, the Bank of Japan indicated at its recent policy meeting that it would ease its monetary policy stance if necessary in the face of increased downside risks. However, the headwinds to further monetary policy easing may be substantial, as its effectiveness is in doubt and the drawbacks of maintaining an ultra-low interest rate environment over the long term are becoming increasingly apparent—for example, as persistently low yields drag on profitability, the capital ratio of regional banks has fallen from 10.6% in 2015 to 9.7% in 2018. Therefore, the Bank of Japan has very limited room to adjust monetary policy in the near term.  In addition to the uncertainties related to the global monetary policy outlook, the uncertain outcome of future trade negotiations and heightened geopolitical risks are two other major sources of risk to the global growth outlook. In early December, the US government announced that it would not increase the tariff on imports from China within 90 days, and extended the deadline again at the end of February, but whether the two sides can reach a long-term trade agreement remains to be seen. Meanwhile, the trade negotiations between the US and the EU have made little progress at this stage. As the outcomes of these trade negotiations remain uncertain, they may continue to cast a shadow over the global growth outlook. Policy and geopolitical risks are also prominent. In the US, partisan disagreements over border security funding led to a 35-day federal government shutdown from late December 2018 to late January 2019. Although the impact of the shutdown on economic growth should be short-lived, the strained relationship between the Trump administration and the Democrat-controlled House of Representatives may lead to more policy gridlock in the future. In the UK, following the overwhelming rejection of the Theresa May government's Brexit deal in mid-January, risks related to Brexit and its knock-on effects surged, and whether a plan can be devised at the last minute to avoid a disruptive "hard Brexit" remains unknown. Elsewhere, geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, such as the US reimposing sanctions on Iran, may also pose uncertainties for oil prices, thereby affecting the global growth outlook.  In East Asia, after fluctuating repeatedly in the first three quarters of last year, financial markets broadly stabilised in the fourth quarter. The US dollar has stabilised since October, and there have been signs that the Fed is being patient about further interest rate hikes, easing the currency depreciation and fund outflow pressures faced by East Asian economies. A number of currencies in the region rose slightly against the US dollar in the fourth quarter, while portfolio investment flows returned to net inflows (Chart 2.8). Chart 2.8 East Asia: currency indices and fund flows. Although financial markets have been stable, there are increasing signs that the region will face a broad-based slowdown. As the China-US trade conflict weakened global trade momentum, export growth in the region declined, causing real GDP growth in most East Asian economies to slow in the second half of last year. Indeed, the new export orders sub-index of the Purchasing Managers' Index in several regional economies (reflecting short-term external trade performance) has fallen into contractionary territory since the fourth quarter, signalling that short-term growth momentum may slow further (Chart 2.9). Chart 2.9 New export orders indices of the Markit Purchasing Managers' Indices for East Asian economies. In an environment of slowing growth, coupled with the recent drop in oil prices, inflationary pressures in East Asia have eased (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 East Asia: headline inflation and oil prices. As recent inflationary pressures and upward pressures on the US dollar have both been relatively mild, East Asian central banks have no pressing need to raise interest rates, easing the policy dilemma of trading off between promoting economic growth and curbing inflation and fund outflow. However, as private-sector debt in some East Asian countries remains high by emerging market standards, central banks still face the challenge of financial imbalances (Chart 2.11).

The Hong Kong economy softened in the second half of 2018, reflecting slower growth in private consumption and weaker export performance amid the China-US trade conflict. As global growth slows, real GDP growth in 2019 is also expected to moderate. Hong Kong's growth outlook is affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, including trade protectionism, the future direction of US monetary policy, and the economic performance of Mainland China. Domestic inflationary pressures should remain mild in 2019, and the outlook faces potential risks on both the upside and downside. Hong Kong's economic activity softened in the second half of 2018. Specifically, economic activity failed to sustain the strong momentum of the first half, and the real GDP growth rate (quarter-on-quarter) turned slightly negative in the second half (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). On a year-on-year basis, economic growth also slowed, with the growth rate in the fourth quarter at 1.3%, below trend growth, dragging the full-year growth rate down from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018.* Based on the volume index of real GDP compiled on an expenditure basis and adjusted for seasonal factors. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contribution of major expenditure components. The weakening of economic activity was mainly due to consumption and exports being dragged down by the direct or indirect impact of the China-US trade conflict. Perhaps because of increased economic uncertainties and the wealth erosion effect brought about by the adjustment in local asset prices, private consumption growth slowed somewhat (Chart 3.1). Total investment spending declined significantly amid fragile business sentiment. Hong Kong's external merchandise trade performance also worsened, especially after China and the US implemented additional tariffs in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as total imports decelerated faster than total exports, net trade still made a positive contribution to real GDP in the fourth quarter. Box 3 examines Hong Kong's merchandise trade performance in greater detail and explores the near-term outlook and its associated risks. Chart 3.2 Real imports and exports. As economic activity weakened, job growth appears to have slowed in the second half of 2018. Total employment increased by only 0.1% to around 3,873,000 people at the end of 2018, a smaller increase than the 0.8% in the first half of 2018. As output and job growth were weak, labour productivity remained broadly stable, showing no signs of significant improvement. As global economic growth slows further, Hong Kong's economic growth is expected to moderate in 2019. Facing challenges in the external environment, Hong Kong's export performance is expected to remain under pressure. On the domestic front, although a low unemployment rate and rising household income will continue to support private consumption, private consumption growth is expected to slow, partly affected by weaker consumer confidence and the wealth erosion effect caused by the earlier adjustment in asset prices. As for fixed capital formation, the outlook may become more uncertain. Although building and construction activities are expected to grow steadily as housing supply increases, businesses may become more cautious about capital investment as economic uncertainties rise. Business sentiment indicators such as the Hong Kong Purchasing Managers' Index continued to hover in contractionary territory, and the forecast of future economic growth based on this index signals a further slowdown in year-on-year growth of real GDP in the near term. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of between 2% and 3% in 2019, while the latest growth forecasts from private-sector analysts range from 1.5% to 2.7%. Hong Kong's growth outlook is affected by the various uncertainties and risks described in the previous two chapters. Although domestic inflationary pressures have continued to build up in recent months, they remain at a mild level. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index recorded increases of 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters of 2018 respectively, higher than the average increase of 2.4% in the first half. The three-month-on-three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also picked up recently, rising from 2.5% in July 2018 to 2.6% in January 2019 (Chart 3.3). The slight rise in inflation momentum was driven by increases in the prices of certain services. The growth in newly signed residential rentals earlier and the accelerating rise in the prices of meals out continued to push up services inflation (Chart 3.4). However, labour cost pressures over the past few quarters remained broadly mild (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Different indicators reflecting consumer price inflation. Chart 3.4 Composite consumer price index rental component and market rentals. Chart 3.5 Unit labour cost and per capita wages. Looking ahead, domestic inflationary pressures should remain mild in 2019. This mainly reflects weakening domestic growth drivers. However, the earlier upward trend in residential rentals will continue to be transmitted to consumer price inflation. The market consensus forecasts a mild headline inflation rate of 2.2% for the full year, while the Government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5%. The above inflation outlook faces risks on both the upside and downside. On the downside risks, the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate remained at around 2.8%, the lowest level in over 20 years (Chart 3.6). If the labour market deteriorates unexpectedly, the current near-zero output gap would turn negative, potentially exerting additional downward pressures on inflation. On the other hand, if China-US trade tensions ease, leading to better-than-expected local economic performance, domestic inflation could be pushed higher. Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate. The China-US trade conflict gradually intensified in the second half of 2018: the US imposed 25% tariffs on goods worth US$34 billion and US$16 billion imported from Mainland China on 6 July and 23 August respectively. Immediately following these two moves, Mainland China responded by imposing 25% tariffs on an equivalent value of US goods. The US escalated again on 24 September, imposing a 10% tariff on goods worth US$200 billion imported from Mainland China. Mainland China immediately responded by imposing tariffs of 5% to 10% on US$60 billion of US goods. Thereafter, the two countries entered negotiations to avoid further tariff increases. As Hong Kong has always been an entrepôt between these two economies, the tariff increases will inevitably have a direct impact on Hong Kong through trade channels. Therefore, the China-US trade dispute has important implications for Hong Kong's macroeconomic and financial stability. This Box reviews Hong Kong's recent merchandise trade performance and explores its near-term outlook. We will also attempt to use more granular data to distinguish trade goods directly affected by the tariff increases, so as to examine the impact of the tariff increases in greater detail. To analyse the impact of the tariffs, we first extracted six sets of data on Hong Kong's re-exports, which were respectively affected by the various rounds of tariff increases described in the previous section. In the first two rounds of tariff increases, the US mainly imposed tariffs on capital goods and semi-finished products, while Mainland China mainly targeted agricultural products, chemicals, medical equipment and energy equipment. In the third round of tariffs, the range of affected goods expanded to cover more consumer goods. For brevity, we correspondingly named the goods affected by these three rounds of tariff increases as List 1, List 2 and List 3. After collecting these more granular trade data, we focused on analysing the year-on-year changes in Hong Kong's re-export values to adjust for the impact of seasonal factors. In addition, readers should also be cautious when analysing the data for September 2018, as trade activity in that month was disrupted to some extent by super typhoon Mangkhut. Overall, the analysis results in this section should only be regarded as preliminary evidence of the impact of the tariff increases. Hong Kong re-exports originating from Mainland China and affected by tariffs: shortly after the tariff increases, the relevant goods re-exported from Mainland China through Hong Kong to the US appear to have decreased significantly or slowed in growth (Chart B3.1). For example, the re-export growth of List 1 and List 2 slowed in the first month after the tariff increases, while re-exports of List 3 recorded negative growth. In addition, re-exports of all three lists recorded negative growth in December. Chart B3.1 Value of goods re-exported from Mainland China through Hong Kong to the US in 2018. Hong Kong re-exports originating from the US and affected by tariffs: by contrast, goods re-exported from the US through Hong Kong to Mainland China performed differently (Chart B3.2). Re-exports of List 1 appeared to decrease significantly in the months following the tariff increases, but rebounded towards the end of the year. Re-exports of List 2 remained at negative growth levels for most of the year, while the growth of List 3 appeared broadly stable. Chart B3.2 Value of goods re-exported from the US through Hong Kong to Mainland China in 2018. Front-loading: since there is a time lag between the announcement and the eventual implementation of tariffs (or simply due to the threat of tariff increases), businesses may increase shipments of affected goods before the expected effective date of the tariffs. In fact, some data and news reports indicate that such front-loading behaviour was quite common. Some private-sector analysts also believe that this behaviour was part of the reason for the strong performance of overall trade figures before the tariff increases. The more granular trade data show that some signs of front-loading appeared in certain tariff list goods, but this seems to involve only goods re-exported from Mainland China to the US (Chart B3.1). The re-export growth rates of List 1 and List 2 both rose in the months before their respective tariffs took effect. On the other hand, the growth rate of re-exports from the US through Hong Kong to Mainland China (Chart B3.2) showed no evident front-loading behaviour by businesses. Hong Kong re-exports not affected by tariff increases: it is worth noting that Hong Kong re-exports (in value terms) directly affected by the tariff increases accounted for only about 4% to 5% of Hong Kong's total re-exports. To gain a more complete understanding of Hong Kong's trade performance, we should also examine re-exports not affected by the tariff increases. We found that re-exports not affected by the tariff increases recorded negative growth in both of the last two months of 2018 (Chart B3.3). In addition, the growth of tariff-affected re-exports (red line) fell markedly more sharply from the third quarter onwards, reflecting the significant impact of the tariffs. The slowdown in the growth of re-exports not affected by the tariff increases partly reflects a broader weakening in external demand. As trade tensions continue to cause increased uncertainties, global financing conditions tighten, and geopolitical risks rise, external demand may come under more broad-based pressure. In particular, the trade conflict has already dragged down global economic sentiment and activity, as reflected in the adjustments in major equity markets. Import demand from other economies has consequently been dragged down, restraining Hong Kong's external trade performance. Chart B3.3 Value of Hong Kong's re-exports in 2018. Even if China-US trade tensions ease, the near-term outlook for Hong Kong's merchandise trade remains challenging. Global economic growth may slow in 2019 (see Chapter 2), which is set to further restrain Hong Kong's export performance. Various business sentiment indicators show that businesses, regardless of size, are pessimistic about their business outlook (Chart B3.4), with business sentiment in the trade sector particularly weak. Other trade-related industries such as logistics may also be affected. Chart B3.4 Business outlook survey of Hong Kong's import and export industry.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trade as liquidity tightened amid expectations of seasonal funding demand. Entering 2019, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually softened, partly due to corporations repatriating funds raised from IPOs and the market rebuilding carry trade positions, triggering the weak-side CU in March. Nevertheless, Hong Kong dollar trading remained smooth and orderly. HIBORs generally rose in the second half of 2018, reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes and seasonal funding demand, before easing back in January 2019. Looking ahead, in the face of uncertainties such as persistent US-China trade tensions, Brexit negotiations, and a less predictable pace of US monetary policy normalisation, HKD fund flows may become more volatile. If the interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar remains wide, market carry trade activities may continue, causing the Hong Kong dollar to stay soft for some time and possibly triggering the weak-side CU again, which is in line with the design of the LERS. Following the triggering of the weak-side CU in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate deviated from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499, until the Hong Kong dollar again triggered the weak-side CU a total of four times in March 2019 (as of 19 March) (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate rose briefly in September, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trade amid tightened liquidity, but subsequently declined gradually in October. The Hong Kong dollar stabilised again after November, as year-end funding demand drove liquidity tightening, leading to the unwinding of carry trade. Entering 2019, the spot exchange rate weakened, partly reflecting corporations repatriating funds raised from IPOs and the market rebuilding carry trade positions. As the interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar widened after the year-end, it triggered market participants' carry trade activities of buying US dollars and selling Hong Kong dollars, driving the Hong Kong dollar to gradually weaken, and the weak-side CU was triggered again in March. Despite the triggering of the weak-side CU, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. The Aggregate Balance had been maintained at around HK$76 billion since August (Chart 4.2), and after the weak-side CU was triggered in March, it declined slightly to HK$70.9 billion (as of 19 March). The HKD funds flowing out since April 2018 accounted for only a small portion of the around HK$1 trillion that had flowed in since 2008. Looking ahead, in the face of uncertainties such as persistent US-China trade tensions, Brexit negotiations, and a less predictable pace of US monetary policy normalisation, fund flow volatility may intensify. Both fund outflow and the possible triggering of the weak-side CU are normal operations under the LERS. Despite the ongoing US interest rate normalisation process and the repeated triggering of the weak-side CU from April to August, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2018. The HKD Monetary Base contracted slightly by 0.7% in the second half, standing at HK$1,632.9 billion at the end of 2018 (Chart 4.4). The contraction in the Monetary Base was mainly due to the triggering of the weak-side CU in August 2018, which led to a decline in the Aggregate Balance from HK$109.5 billion at the end of June 2018 to HK$76.4 billion at the end of 2018, while the Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased slightly. The HKD Monetary Base remained largely stable in the first two months of 2019, with the Aggregate Balance showing no significant change since August. Subsequently, due to the triggering of the weak-side CU in March, the Aggregate Balance declined slightly to around HK$70.9 billion (as of 19 March). The balance of RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew slightly faster than the 2.6% increase in the first half, rising 3.7% in the second half to RMB657.7 billion at the end of 2018 (Chart 4.11 and Table 4.B). Benefiting mainly from an increase in net interest income, the profitability of retail banks continued to improve in the second half of 2018 compared with the same period in 2017. Their capital and liquidity positions also remained sound. Reflecting the upward pressure on HKD interbank interest rates and retail deposit rates amid the normalization of US interest rates, the overall HKD funding cost of retail banks rose notably, though it remained at a relatively low level. Amid an uncertain external environment, bank credit contracted moderately in the second half of 2018. Nevertheless, credit growth has shown signs of stabilizing since November, and asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will face multiple headwinds due to the persistent uncertainty over China-US trade relations, the global economic slowdown, the uncertain pace of the US monetary policy tightening cycle, and geopolitical risks. In view of the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should remain vigilant about the impact on the credit risk of their related corporate loans arising from a possible further deterioration in the external environment.  The overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 14.3% compared with the same period in 2017, while return on assets rose from 1.14% to 1.23% (Chart 5.1). This strong performance was mainly attributable to the substantial growth in net interest income, which was sufficient to offset the increases in loan impairment provisions and operating expenses. For 2018 as a whole, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 19.4%, while return on assets rose from 1.16% in 2017 to 1.27%. Looking ahead, the increased uncertainty in the external environment may cloud banks' profit outlook. In particular, against the backdrop of a slowdown in global economic growth, the persistent uncertainty over China-US trade relations may dampen business confidence and reduce demand for bank credit. Should this lead to a significant decline in loans and a deterioration in asset quality, it may weigh on banks' profitability. The coronavirus outbreak that erupted since early 2020 hit both demand and supply simultaneously, posing challenges to the global economy that differed from previous crises. Although major central banks and some governments have rolled out stimulus measures since early March to counter the economic shocks brought about by the outbreak, financial markets remained volatile, and global financing conditions also tightened. Despite uncertainties in both the external and local environments, Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and orderly. Amid a stronger Hong Kong dollar exchange rate, a stable Aggregate Balance, and moderate growth in total deposits, no significant outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. After a moderate rebound in the first half of 2019, growth in total loans slowed in the second half. The residential property market softened generally since mid-2019, though the trend was somewhat volatile. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face a number of downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future China-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social incidents. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and personal debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, global economic growth has shown preliminary signs of stabilising, benefiting from major central banks stepping up their policy-easing efforts, the easing of China-US trade tensions, and the reduced risk of a "no-deal Brexit" in the UK. However, since late January, the growing number of global coronavirus infection cases has raised market concerns and triggered sharp volatility in global financial markets. To respond to the evolving risks of the outbreak, several major central banks cut interest rates substantially and expanded liquidity tools, while some governments also introduced targeted measures to support the real economy. Nevertheless, amid rising credit spreads and plunging stock markets, global financing conditions tightened. Looking ahead, downside risks to the global economic outlook have increased. The coronavirus outbreak will hit global economic activity, and the extent of the economic shock will depend on the severity and persistence of the outbreak. In the medium term, relations between the US and its major trading partners may become tense again, and the UK's post-Brexit trade negotiations with the EU may also prove difficult. Weak global demand continued to weigh on economic growth in East Asia. Exports from East Asia to various major destinations, including the US, European economies, and Mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019. Some major telecommunications equipment exporters in the region recently reported an increase in earnings, but whether the technology product cycle will rebound broadly remains to be seen. Financial markets reacted positively to the China-US Phase One trade agreement announced in December 2019, and the trade truce reduced uncertainties in global trade to some extent. Nevertheless, East Asia will continue to face headwinds such as weak firms’ earnings and high private-sector leverage ratio. At the same time, the coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that the region's economy may come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. Travel bans imposed by many economies in the region may hit tourism in Asia, especially economies that are more reliant on tourism service exports. As the region's supply chains are closely linked to Mainland China, manufacturing may also be affected by the outbreak. As for Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the China-US Phase One trade agreement helps to temporarily reduce the external uncertainties facing the Mainland economy, downward pressures remain amid the impact of the coronavirus outbreak, the ongoing economic rebalancing, and the global economic slowdown. The Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2019 made stabilising the economy the priority for 2020, while also focusing on the control of financial risks. The latest consensus forecast indicates that Mainland economic growth will slow to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, Mainland authorities continued to announce targeted monetary and fiscal policies to support the private sector, especially small private enterprises. Despite these measures, some media reports and market analysts pointed out that private industrial enterprises may have faced declining shareholders' equity in recent years, which is regarded as a sign of "private sector retreat". Box 2 studies the drivers of equity changes among Mainland industrial enterprises using 2018 listed corporates data and finds that private enterprises or small enterprises were not inherently more susceptible to downsizing or "retreat". Although the study found that negative profits were the biggest driver, other factors, especially structural factors, are also worth noting (see Box 2 for details). Local economic activity contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. Real GDP declined in each of the past three quarters, indicating that the local economy had entered a recession. Dragged down by this, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the whole of 2019, worse than the 2.9% growth in 2018, and the first annual contraction since 2009. The slowdown in local demand, especially the contraction in private consumption, was the main factor dragging down GDP in the second half of 2019. Local social incidents severely affected consumption activity, leading to a weak economic outlook, which in turn lowered consumer and business sentiment. With the renewed escalation of China-US trade frictions, the slowdown in global economic growth, and the severe downturn in inbound tourism, Hong Kong's external trade performance remained sluggish. Given the significant headwinds facing the economy, the government rolled out several rounds of economic stimulus measures between August and December 2019. To give banks greater room to step up their support for the local economy and to help smooth the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October a reduction of the banks' countercyclical capital buffer ratio from 2.5% to 2.0%, which could allow banks to release an additional HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion in lending capacity to enterprises, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, and the outbreak has also recently posed significant downside risks. As industries such as retail, accommodation services, food services, tourism, and transportation have yet to recover from the disruptions caused by the social incidents, the outbreak will deliver a double blow to these industries. However, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide assistance to households and enterprises (especially SMEs), including distributing a one-off cash payment to adult permanent residents and providing enterprises with special concessionary low-interest loans with a 100% government guarantee under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. On 16 March 2020, the HKMA further reduced the banks' countercyclical capital buffer ratio from 2.0% to 1.0%, which will give banks greater room to step up their support for the local economy, especially industries and individuals under greater short-term pressure due to the impact of the outbreak. By GDP component, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak due to fragile consumer and business sentiment. Although government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to be relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. In terms of external factors, the China-US Phase One trade agreement is expected to have a slightly positive impact on the local economy in the short term. However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may cause disruptions to supply chains in the region and a slowdown in cross-border economic activities (such as tourism), thereby constraining Hong Kong's export performance. The government forecasts that real GDP growth in 2020 will range between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average growth forecast by international institutions and private-sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the slowdown in global economic growth, China-US trade relations, Mainland China's economic performance, and local social incidents. The labour market faced greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020, with total employment declining, the unemployment rate rising, and the real payroll index also falling year on year. Specifically, the unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.7% in February 2020, partly reflecting the impact of the social incidents and the outbreak on the retail, accommodation, and food services industries. Looking ahead, given the weak economic outlook and the coronavirus outbreak, the unemployment rate will climb further. Box 3 will explore the recent developments and short-term outlook of the labour market in greater detail. Local inflationary pressures continued to build up through the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to the impact of rising fresh pork prices; subsequently, as economic activity weakened, inflation momentum gradually slowed. Given weak economic conditions, the consolidation of residential rentals, and mild imported inflation, inflation is expected to ease in the short term. Market consensus forecasts that the headline inflation rate in 2020 will range between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5%. Supported by increased equity-related demand for the Hong Kong dollar (including IPOs), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened gradually since mid-October 2019. In December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened further, partly due to buoyant IPO activity and partly due to the tightening of liquidity near year-end, which prompted the unwinding of Hong Kong dollar short positions. After the Lunar New Year holidays, liquidity conditions eased somewhat, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened slightly near the end of February. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly during the review period, without triggering the CUs. The Aggregate Balance remained stable at around HK$54 billion. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, short-term HKD interbank interest rates have been volatile, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand as well as increased capital market activities such as IPOs. Box 4 studies how market attention to future IPO activity affects the 3-month HIBORs. Meanwhile, the composite interest rate rose gradually from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020, reflecting banks' continued increases in preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funds. As some banks raised the caps on the rates set with reference to the Best Lending Rates, the average lending rate for new mortgages rose to around 2.6% in October, but as the Best Lending Rates in the market were lowered from November, the average lending rate for new mortgages fell slightly to around 2.5% by January 2020. Amid a stronger Hong Kong dollar exchange rate, a stable Aggregate Balance, and moderate growth in total deposits, no significant outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. However, we need to monitor the impact of any further deterioration of the coronavirus outbreak amid an uncertain external environment. Hong Kong has ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system, and the HKMA has the ability, resources, and determination to cope with capital outflows and to maintain monetary and financial stability in Hong Kong. During the review period, amid market anticipation of a China-US trade agreement, both the offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates strengthened, but faced downward pressure since late January 2020 due to the outbreak of the coronavirus. In late 2019, the CNH generally traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi, and the discount briefly widened at the end of January 2020, but the differential remained moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong's CNH liquidity pool rebounded slightly after a small decline in the previous review period. As at the end of January 2020, RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit balances rose to RMB637.4 billion. Towards the end of 2019, global economic activity showed signs of stabilisation, raising market hopes for a global economic recovery. However, since late January 2020, the continued rise in global coronavirus infection cases has dashed hopes of a recovery, deepening investor concerns over a global economic recession and triggering a sell-off in global financial markets. To address the economic shock, major central banks and some governments have rolled out stimulus measures since early March. In view of the spread of the pandemic, downside risks to the outlook for global economic growth have increased. In East Asia, weak global demand since the second half of 2019 has clouded the outlook for economies in the region. The coronavirus outbreak is expected to weigh on economic growth in the region in the near term, with the tourism industry hit particularly hard. On the other hand, the East Asian region also continues to face the challenges of weak corporate profitability and elevated private-sector leverage ratios. As for Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 owing to weak domestic demand and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the "phase one" trade agreement between the US and China helped temporarily reduce external uncertainties, downward pressures persist amid the coronavirus outbreak, continued economic rebalancing and the global economic slowdown, while the monetary and fiscal policy responses adopted by the authorities will provide some cushion. Amid persistent trade tensions and policy uncertainty, manufacturing and investment remained sluggish, and global economic growth was still lacklustre in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, economic growth showed preliminary signs of stabilisation early in the final quarter (Chart 2.1), partly benefiting from the earlier policy easing by the Fed and the ECB, as well as the easing of global trade tensions following the signing of the "phase one" trade agreement between the US and China. Chart 2.1 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index. However, since late January, the continued rise in global coronavirus infection cases and the subsequent economic shock have sparked market concerns, resulting in a sell-off in global financial markets (Chart 2.2). Given that Mainland China is a major global export destination and occupies an important position in the global supply chain, when the pandemic disrupts production activities on the Mainland and drags down its economic growth, it will generate significant spillover effects that may spread across the globe (Chart 2.3). Since late February, the surge in coronavirus infection cases outside Mainland China may intensify disruptions to the supply chain and pose the risk of directly dragging down local economic activity. 5 Chart 2.2 MSCI All Country World Index and Bloomberg Barclays Global Corporate Bond Index Option-Adjusted Spread. To address the potentially severe economic shock from the pandemic, some central banks (including the Fed, the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England) have cut interest rates since early March, while some governments have introduced targeted measures to support households and businesses. Nevertheless, financial markets still face enormous sell-off pressure, leading to a marked tightening in global financing conditions, which may in turn intensify the downward pressures on the global economy (Chart 2.4). In addition to developments related to the pandemic, other downside risks and uncertainties also loom over the global economic outlook. In particular, on trade tensions, although policy risks have declined following the "phase one" trade agreement between the US and China, subsequent negotiations may prove difficult given the many thorny structural issues that remain to be resolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the EU and the UK are not expected to go smoothly, thereby sustaining uncertainties following Brexit. In addition, oil prices have plunged sharply since March, which will put pressure on major oil-exporting emerging market economies. In East Asia, real economic activity remained lacklustre in the second half of 2019 owing to weak global demand. The East Asian region's exports to various major destinations such as the US, European economies and Mainland China remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Chart 2.5). Although there are preliminary signs that the downcycle in the region's technology products is bottoming out and rebounding, including reports from large electronics companies in the region of improved profitability at the end of 2019, 6 whether the region's technology product exports will stage a genuine rebound remains to be seen. Chart 2.5 East Asia: merchandise exports to major destinations. Sluggish economic growth and trade uncertainties have also weighed on investor sentiment, with gross fixed capital investment in most East Asian economies declining in 2019 (Chart 2.6), which may affect the region's potential economic growth over the long term. To support economic growth in an environment of moderate inflation, the central banks of Indonesia, the Philippines and Korea, after cutting rates in the first half of 2019, lowered their policy rates again in the second half, while the Bank of Thailand also lowered its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Chart 2.6 East Asia: gross fixed capital formation. The coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that economies in the region may come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. As many economies in the region have imposed entry and exit restrictions on Mainland China, the tourism industry has borne the brunt, with economies that rely more heavily on Mainland Chinese tourists and tourism service exports being more affected by the pandemic (Chart 2.7). A prolonged and intensified pandemic would also affect the region's supply chains that are closely linked to Mainland China. Chart 2.7 East Asia: tourism exports and Chinese tourists. In the near term, the pandemic will continue to affect economic activity and investor sentiment. Drawing on the experience of the 2003 SARS outbreak, these effects may be transient, but the actual situation will depend on the severity and extent of the pandemic's spread, as well as the effectiveness of government actions to contain the outbreak. At the same time, East Asian economies also face multiple headwinds. First, although the market expects corporate profitability to deteriorate in the near term (Chart 2.8), accommodative global monetary conditions have encouraged yield-seeking activities, pushing up asset prices without fundamental support. As a result, the region's equity markets are more susceptible to shifts in investor sentiment. Chart 2.8 Expected earnings of benchmark equity index constituents. Second, weak corporate profitability and economic growth may make it more difficult for private-sector entities in the region to repay debt. While declining local interest rates can provide breathing room for indebted companies and households, they may also sow the seeds of further debt accumulation. Moreover, as discussed in Box 1, as more index-tracking funds flow into the region's financial markets, the risk of debt overhang for private-sector entities may also intensify, although this impact may be limited to companies with more solid financial foundations and their long-term borrowings. Third, in terms of external factors, East Asian economies may also face increasing risks in the face of an increasingly protectionist US trade policy. Despite recent progress in the "phase one" trade agreement between the US and China, trade tensions between the two countries persist as fundamental trade issues between them remain unresolved. As evidenced by the growing net trade surpluses of several economies in the region with the US (Chart 2.9), multinational companies, in order to circumvent tariffs, may continue to seek additional sourcing channels outside China-centric supply chains. As of November 2019, the cumulative net trade surplus of nine emerging Asian economies (excluding China) with the US had risen to around 167 billion US dollar. If net trade surpluses with the US continue to widen, the relevant Asian economies may become the next target of trade conflicts; for example, the US government imposed massive tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam in July 2019. 7 In view of this, despite the US-China trade truce, the region's trade outlook remains highly uncertain. Chart 2.9 Net trade in goods with the US. Over the past decade, the deepening integration of international financial markets has led to a marked increase in global cross-border portfolio investment flows. A recent study shows that up to 70% of these cross-border investment flows are driven by index-driven funds. 8 Index-driven funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices (commonly referred to as passive funds), but also funds that are actively managed with reference to investment indices. 9 By introducing overseas investors that the relevant economies would otherwise be unable to attract or access, these funds help promote the development of financial markets in emerging market economies. Consequently, such funds enable emerging market economies to diversify their investor base, which is conducive to the long-term growth and stability of the market. However, is there really such a thing as a free lunch? In the case of passive bond funds, the market is concerned that such fund investments may weaken the fiscal discipline of the corporate bonds issuers in which they invest, thereby leading to elevated leverage levels among the relevant companies. 10 In addition, some argue that the growth of index-driven funds in recent years has amplified the volatility of global portfolio investment flows, making emerging market economies—already highly sensitive to global factors and influenced by other common factors—even more vulnerable. 11 This box assesses the impact of index-driven investment on financial stability with respect to these two propositions. In accordance with the weight of constituent bonds within the benchmark index, passive bond funds allocate their investment capital to the relevant bonds. Therefore, relative to actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions adopted by passive bond funds may leave the issuers of index-constituent bonds with little incentive to act in the interests of the fund investors. 13 Worse still, from a financial stability perspective, such behaviour may fuel excessive borrowing, posing significant risks to the credit standing and debt repayment abilities of the corporate sector of emerging market economies, whose leverage ratios have risen sharply since the global financial crisis (Chart B1.1). Chart B1.1 Corporate leverage in emerging market economies. Using the weight of each emerging market economy's corporations within a mainstream index tracking emerging market economy corporate bonds as an estimate of the extent to which their bonds are invested in by passive bond funds, 14 we find that an increase in such investment would push up the long-term (rather than short-term) leverage ratios of the corporate issuers of the relevant bonds. The solid blue bars in Chart B1.2 indicate the estimated effect. In addition to promoting the development of the corporate bond market in emerging market economies, the expanded long-term bond investor base brought about by passive bond funds is also conducive to the development of corporations in emerging market economies. We also find that the above effect has a significant impact only on emerging market economy corporations with more solid fundamentals (particularly stronger debt repayment abilities and lower leverage ratios) (the solid green bars in Chart B1.2). Facing higher costs of financial distress, highly leveraged corporations or those with weaker debt repayment abilities seem, in contrast, not to fall further into a debt trap as a result of passive bond fund investment. In summary, the above research suggests that the growth of passive bond fund investment may not substantially increase the risks to the debt repayment abilities of the corporate sector in emerging market economies.

Owing to weaker private consumption, reduced investment spending and lacklustre export performance, the Hong Kong economy contracted in the second half of 2019 and slipped into its first recession since 2009. Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face considerable challenges, and the coronavirus epidemic has also recently brought about significant downside risks. The economic outlook is being affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, including slowing global economic growth, China-US trade relations, the economic performance of Mainland China, and developments in local social incidents. Given the various headwinds facing the economy, the unemployment rate is likely to climb further in 2020. Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease somewhat, though the outlook faces potential risks on both the upside and downside. The Hong Kong economy contracted markedly in the second half of 2019. On a year-on-year basis, real GDP contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters respectively (Table 3.A). Dragged down by the economic contraction in the second half of the year, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the full year, worse than the 2.9% growth in 2018, and was also the first annual contraction recorded since the global financial crisis in 2009. Figure 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contributions of major expenditure components On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity slowed markedly in the second half of the year (Figure 3.1). Specifically, real GDP fell successively by 0.4%, 3.0% and 0.3% in the second, third and fourth quarters respectively, indicating that the economy had already entered a recession. On the domestic front, private consumption was the main factor dragging down GDP in the third quarter. Local social incidents severely affected consumption activity, thereby weakening the economic outlook and dealing a blow to consumer confidence, so private consumption contracted markedly starting from the third quarter.33 Owing to increased economic uncertainties and deteriorating business sentiment, total investment spending remained weak and dragged down GDP in the fourth quarter.34 On the external front, as China-US trade tensions intensified, global economic growth weakened and visitor arrivals to Hong Kong plunged sharply, Hong Kong's external trade performance remained sluggish (Figure 3.2).35 Affected by the sharp contraction in exports of services, net exports dragged down GDP in the third quarter but provided support to GDP growth in the fourth quarter, partly reflecting an improvement in the merchandise trade balance. Figure 3.2 Real imports and exports Given the enormous headwinds facing the economy, the Government rolled out several rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to alleviate the financial burden on the public, safeguard employment, and support enterprises, in particular small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and hard-hit sectors such as retail, food services, transport and tourism.36 In order to give banks greater room to step up their support for the local economy and help smooth the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October that it would lower banks' countercyclical capital buffer ratio from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional HKD 200 billion to HKD 300 billion in lending capacity to enterprises, including SMEs. Hong Kong's economic performance in 2020 is expected to face considerable challenges, and the epidemic has also recently brought about significant downside risks. As some sectors have yet to recover from the damage caused by the social incidents, the epidemic will deal a double blow to these sectors. Nevertheless, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide relief to households and enterprises (in particular SMEs), including the disbursement of a one-off cash payout to adult permanent residents and the provision of concessionary low-interest loans with a 100% government guarantee to enterprises under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme".37 On 16 March 2020, the HKMA further lowered banks' countercyclical capital buffer ratio from 2.0% to 1.0%, which will give banks greater room to step up their support for the local economy, particularly for sectors and individuals coming under greater short-term pressure due to the impact of the epidemic. Analysing by the components of GDP, private consumption and investment spending are likely to remain weak owing to fragile consumer and business sentiment. Although government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to be relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the first-phase China-US trade agreement is expected to have a slightly positive impact on the local economy in the short term.38 However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may cause disruptions to regional supply chains and slow down cross-border economic activity (such as tourism), thereby constraining Hong Kong's export performance. The Government forecasts real GDP growth in 2020 to range between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average growth forecast from international institutions and private-sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is affected by numerous uncertainties and risks described in the preceding chapters. The labour market came under greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and climbed further to 3.7% in February 2020 (Figure 3.3). Among them, the unemployment rate for the retail, accommodation and food services sectors rose to a near-decade high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the severe blow caused by the social incidents.39 As economic momentum weakened, total employment fell by 0.5% year-on-year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline to 3,768,800 in February 2020. Among these, the decline in employment came mainly from the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food services and construction sectors. Real wages also fell by 0.3% year-on-year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, in view of the aforementioned weak economic outlook, the labour market will continue to face more challenges, and the unemployment rate is very likely to climb further. Box 3 will explore the recent developments and short-term outlook of the labour market in greater detail. Figure 3.3 Labour market conditions Local inflationary pressures continued to build up to the third quarter of 2019, mainly owing to the effect of rising fresh pork prices; subsequently, as economic activity weakened, inflation momentum also gradually slowed. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index grew by 3.3% in the third quarter, while the increase eased slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The three-month-on-three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also softened from a high of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The slowdown in inflation momentum was due to reduced price pressures on various components of the consumer price index. On tradable goods, rising fresh pork prices kept underlying food inflation notable, though price pressures on consumer goods such as clothing and footwear and durable goods remained mild. On services, as growth in newly signed residential rentals slowed earlier, growth in the rental component of the consumer price index also showed a downward trend (Figure 3.5). Labour cost pressures rose slightly but remained mild over the past few quarters (Figure 3.6). Figure 3.4 Different indicators reflecting consumer price inflation Figure 3.5 Composite consumer price index rental component and market rentals Figure 3.6 Unit labour cost Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease somewhat in the short term. On the domestic front, weak economic conditions and a widening negative output gap will continue to exert downward pressures on local inflation. As residential rentals continue to slow, the housing rental component of inflation should ease further. On the external front, imported inflation is expected to remain mild owing to weak global economic growth and soft energy prices. Market consensus forecasts headline inflation in 2020 to range between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation at 2.5% and headline inflation at 1.7%. This inflation outlook is affected by risk factors on both the upside and downside. On the one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, if the economy deteriorates more severely than expected (for example, due to the persistence of the coronavirus epidemic), inflation may be further dampened. On the other hand, if disruptions to fresh pork supply become more severe, this will bring upward pressure on inflation. Despite the marked slowdown in Hong Kong's economy, the unemployment rate in the first nine months of 2019 remained at a low level of 2.8-2.9%. It was only as the social incidents persisted that the unemployment rate climbed more notably to 3.3% by the end of 2019. Affected by the coronavirus epidemic, the labour market will face greater headwinds in 2020. Against this backdrop, this box analyses the recent developments and short-term outlook of the labour market, including exploring why the overall labour market remained largely resilient in the first three quarters of 2019 (with the unemployment rate barely changing), and what implications this has for future developments. This article also examines some risk factors that may lead to a sharp rise in the unemployment rate. It is worth noting that, partly because adjusting labour demand entails costs, the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator. In fact, the unemployment rate tends to lag the year-on-year growth of real GDP by about two to three quarters (Figure B3.1). This lagging nature can explain why the unemployment rate remained low at about 2.9% when real economic activity deteriorated sharply in the third quarter. Specifically, employment in the financial and business services, public administration, social and personal services sectors continued to grow in 2019, partly offsetting the impact of the decline in employment in the trade and retail sectors (Figure B3.2). Despite the economy entering a recession, Hong Kong's financial system remained sound, and financial activity in areas such as fintech development and new share listings was also very active. These factors may all help support the employment market in the financial and business services sectors. In addition, the public administration, social and personal services sectors, including education, healthcare and social work activities, appear to be less sensitive to the economic cycle. Analysis of correlation coefficients shows that although employment in many sectors is highly correlated with real GDP, the public administration, social and personal services sectors respond more neutrally to the economic cycle. In other words, even if the economy slows, employment in these sectors may not be greatly affected by cyclical factors. As shown in the chart, the labour force participation rate (green bar) exerted downward pressures on the unemployment rate in 2019.41 On the other hand, the increase in employment in the first half of 2019 (purple bar) also helped suppress the unemployment rate. However, the economy contracted markedly in the second half of the year, and the decline in employment exerted upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Taken together, although employment fell during the recession, the lower labour force participation rate helped alleviate the pressure of the rising unemployment rate in the second half of 2019. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has strengthened since October, with the upward momentum strengthening further in December, keeping the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate on the strong side of the CUs Zone in recent months. The strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar came partly from equity-related demand and partly from the unwinding of Hong Kong dollar short positions prompted by tightening liquidity towards year-end. Overall, Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets continued to function smoothly and in an orderly manner. Although in an uncertain external environment, the coronavirus outbreak affecting market sentiment could lead to increased fund flow volatility, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system, and is therefore able to withstand the pressure of fund outflow without affecting the city's financial stability. Supported by increased equity-related demand for the Hong Kong dollar (including IPO), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually strengthened since mid-October (Chart 4.1). Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar strengthened further, and from mid-December to February, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained on the strong side of the CUs Zone. The strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate was partly attributable to buoyant IPO activities and partly to the unwinding of Hong Kong dollar short positions prompted by tightening liquidity towards year-end. After the Lunar New Year holidays, liquidity conditions eased somewhat and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly, closing at 7.7956 on 28 February. Overall, during the review period, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to function smoothly and in an orderly manner. As neither the strong-side nor the weak-side CU was triggered during the review period, the Aggregate Balance remained unchanged at around HK$54 billion (Chart 4.2). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was very small and therefore had limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index, the movement of the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index broadly followed that of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates In measuring Hong Kong's fund flows, it is essential to distinguish between two distinct but interrelated concepts of fund flows: (1) HKD fund flows; and (2) cross-border fund flows. HKD fund flows focus on the monetary dimension of fund flows and help assess monetary stability, especially under the LERS. On the other hand, cross-border fund flows focus on the movement of funds across geographical regions through Hong Kong's banking system, which helps assess the stability of Hong Kong's overall financial system. The two concepts of fund flows require different monitoring indicators. In monitoring HKD fund flows, attention should be paid to the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate and the Aggregate Balance. If the public or investors convert a large amount of their Hong Kong dollar assets into foreign currency assets, demand for the Hong Kong dollar will naturally decline, leading to a weakening of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate. Under the LERS, if the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakens to the weak-side CU level of HK$7.85 per US dollar, the HKMA stands ready to buy Hong Kong dollars upon banks' request, and the Aggregate Balance will subsequently decrease. Since April 2019, the Aggregate Balance has remained broadly unchanged, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has been on the strong side of the CUs Zone in recent months, so no significant fund outflow from the Hong Kong dollar was observed during the review period. In monitoring cross-border fund flows, Hong Kong's total bank deposits are a useful indicator. When there is a large fund outflow from Hong Kong's banking system, bank deposits will inevitably decrease. During the review period, total deposits grew at a moderate pace, indicating that no significant cross-border fund outflow occurred. Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets continued to function smoothly and in an orderly manner, indicating that the impact of the coronavirus outbreak on the city's monetary environment remained limited. Nevertheless, we need to closely monitor the risks posed by the coronavirus outbreak. Hong Kong possesses ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system, and the HKMA has the ability, resources and determination to cope with fund outflow and maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. Despite the uncertain external environment and the local economic slowdown, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The HKD Monetary Base remained large, rising 4.0% since end-June to HK$1,689.4 billion at end-January 2020 (Chart 4.4). As the CUs were not triggered during this period, the Aggregate Balance remained broadly unchanged at around HK$54 billion. The other components of the Monetary Base, including outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, Certificates of Indebtedness, and government-issued notes and coins in circulation, rose steadily. Amid increasing uncertainties in the global and local economic environment, the profitability of Hong Kong's retail banks recorded a slight decline in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, the capital and liquidity positions of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong and robust by international standards. Asset quality remained healthy by historical standards. Although the growth in total loans slowed somewhat in the second half of last year, it still outpaced deposit growth over the same period during the review period. Correspondingly, the average loan-to-deposit ratios of all AIs, calculated in all currencies, as well as the HKD loan-to-deposit ratio, both increased. However, given that the aggregate balance of the banking system remained stable and deposits remained largely steady, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face a number of downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future direction of US-China trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social incidents. Given the persistent rise in corporate leverage and personal debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify.  In the second half of 2019, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell slightly by 1.5% compared with the same period in 2018. Correspondingly, the return on assets edged down to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, lower than the 1.23% recorded in the same period in 2018 (Chart 5.1). Although the net interest margin of retail banks narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.2), the net interest income of retail banks continued to record moderate growth during the review period. However, both the loan impairment provisions and operating expenses of retail banks increased, resulting in a slight decline in profitability. Looking ahead, a number of downside risk factors in the external and local environment will continue to cast a shadow over banks' profitability outlook. Relevant factors include uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future direction of US-China trade relations, and the intensification of geopolitical tensions. The intensification of these risk factors may dampen the already weak momentum of global economic growth and reduce the demand for bank credit. Given the widespread adoption of accommodative monetary policy by major central banks, the global low interest rate environment may persist, which could exert pressure on banks' future net interest margins. At the local level, local social incidents since mid-2019 have continued to weigh on business investment and market confidence. Against the backdrop of an already weak economic environment, if the situation persists or even intensifies further in the future, it may worsen the outlook for credit demand and banks' asset quality.  In terms of overall market developments, following the HKMA's granting of eight virtual banking licences, the Hong Kong banking sector began to roll out virtual banking services. As these new market participants may seek to increase their market share by attracting new customers through more convenient products and more attractive deposit rates, this may exert upward pressure on the cost of funding of existing banks. Although the short-term impact may remain moderate given the currently limited business scale of virtual banks, the long-term impact may depend on whether existing banks accelerate the adoption of financial technology to maintain competitiveness. The results of Feature Article 5 show that the extent to which Hong Kong banks adopt financial technology is statistically correlated with improvements in their cost efficiency and profitability.
