The rollout of COVID-19 vaccines brought hope for reopening economies and boosted the global growth outlook. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary policy-easing, financial markets repeatedly reached new highs. However, the global outlook remained clouded by uncertainties, and the pace of recovery across economies was expected to be uneven. Over the medium term, the disconnect between financial markets and the real economy, elevated debt levels, and the lasting economic scars inflicted by the pandemic will pose challenges for policymakers going forward. The HKD foreign exchange and money markets continued to function smoothly and in an orderly manner. The HKD traded close to the strong-side CUs against the US dollar, driven mainly by equity-related demand. During the review period, total deposits increased, and there were no signs of large-scale fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Partly reflecting weak economic activity and lower credit demand amid the recurring pandemic, total lending in the banking sector declined slightly in the second half of the year, yet still recorded a mild increase for 2020 as a whole. Meanwhile, the residential property market remained broadly stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties over the pace of economic recovery and persistent geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges to Hong Kong's banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic weakens the repayment ability of corporates and households, the banking sector should continue to closely monitor the impact of relevant downside risks on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies reopened, but a resurgence of COVID-19 infections from the fourth quarter caused global growth to slow again. Nonetheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development at the end of 2020, the market expected the pandemic would eventually end, favouring a return to normality and accelerated growth for the global economy. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary policy-easing, global financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021, even as signs of a disconnect from the real economy began to emerge. Against this backdrop, uncertainties will continue to cloud the global economic outlook. Whether vaccines can be widely distributed remains to be seen. Meanwhile, supply bottlenecks and the earlier aggressive easing may lead to higher-than-expected inflation, which in turn may require central banks to scale back monetary policy-easing earlier, ending the market's expectation of a "lower for longer" monetary policy. In the long run, policymakers will need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures, and address the many economic legacy issues triggered by the pandemic, including elevated global debt and lasting economic scars. In East Asia, supported by a recovery in export demand, GDP growth improved in the second half of 2020. With increased risk appetite, portfolio investment inflows into the region rebounded, and search-for-yield activity re-emerged. Despite these positive developments, East Asia still faces persistent uncertainties brought by the pandemic. First, in the global competition for vaccine procurement, the region's less-developed economies may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hampering the recovery of their tourism and services industries. Second, uncertainties may arise regarding vaccine supply, coverage, or effectiveness, and combined with weaker fiscal positions of governments in the region, this may worsen market sentiment and trigger a reversal of fund flows. As for Mainland China, with consumption activity gradually returning to normal, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020. For 2020 as a whole, the Mainland economy grew by 2.3%, the only major economy to record positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook still largely depends on the development of the pandemic and changes in US-China tensions. The latest consensus forecasts show that the Mainland economy will grow by 8.4% in 2021. The renminbi depreciated for several months in early 2020, but subsequently strengthened over the remainder of the year as economic recovery accelerated, the US dollar weakened, and the Mainland bond market recorded strong inflows. Detailed studies show that during the COVID-19 outbreak, fundamentals rather than market sentiment played a more important role in driving renminbi exchange rate movements (for details, please refer to Box 1). The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real GDP remained far below pre-pandemic levels. With a slight increase in local demand and a further expansion in exports of goods, seasonally adjusted real GDP began to recover in the third quarter, ending five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real GDP also narrowed markedly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to about 3% in the second half. However, for 2020 as a whole, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record, and the first time in history that two consecutive years of decline were recorded following the 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest GDP data by sector show that the contraction in consumption- and tourism-related industries was worse than the overall economy amid the pandemic. To address the ongoing pandemic, the Government launched two further rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund in the second half of 2020 to help sectors and citizens affected by the pandemic and to enhance Hong Kong's capacity to combat the epidemic. The Government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures to boost the economy in the recent 2021/22 Budget, including a one-off HKD 5,000 electronic consumption voucher and a 100%-guaranteed personal special loan for the unemployed. The HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, announced in March 2021 that the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme would be extended to October of the same year, and announced an extension of the repayment period for trade finance loans under the scheme. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will still face considerable challenges in early 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong's exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes. With breakthroughs in vaccine development, the market expected that the novel coronavirus pandemic would eventually come to an end and that the global economy would be able to accelerate its growth afterwards. Coupled with the anticipated "lower for longer" global monetary policy, investors were not deterred by the resurgence of the pandemic at the end of 2020, and financial markets rose to new highs at the beginning of 2021. However, the market's eager expectations were disconnected from a macroeconomic environment that remained full of challenges. Should the economic recovery be weaker than desired, or should support measures be withdrawn earlier than expected (for example, due to inflation exceeding expectations), asset prices could become volatile. Looking ahead, policymakers will need to grapple with the challenge of when to withdraw policy support, as well as to address the many problems left behind by the pandemic, including elevated debt levels and long-lasting economic scarring. Persistent uncertainties surrounding the pandemic continue to cast a shadow over the economic recovery in the East Asia region, where the less-developed emerging market economies within the region may face greater challenges in procuring and distributing vaccines. Any setbacks in the progress of vaccination programmes could reverse the current optimistic sentiment and destabilise capital inflows and financial markets. As for Mainland China, with consumption activities gradually returning to normal, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020. Looking ahead, the growth outlook remains fraught with uncertainty and will depend largely on the development of the pandemic and changes in US-China tensions. Accordingly, the government announced that it would continue to maintain a supportive policy stance and emphasised the importance of controlling systemic risks. Benefiting from the purchasing power unleashed by the reopening of the economy, most major economies recorded better-than-expected real GDP growth in the third quarter of 2020. However, since the fourth quarter, novel coronavirus infection figures have climbed again, prompting governments to reinstate lockdowns and social distancing measures, and global growth momentum weakened once more. At the end of 2020, more transmissible variants of the virus emerged and subsequently spread across the world, making the situation even more severe. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of multiple vaccines for use at the end of 2020, the market expected that the pandemic would eventually come to an end, and that the global economy would return to normal and accelerate its growth. Another driving force supporting the global economic recovery came from ongoing policy stimulus measures, including major central banks committing to a "lower for longer" monetary policy amid weak inflation, as well as sustained fiscal easing in major advanced economies, particularly the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Correspondingly, the International Monetary Fund revised its 2021 global GDP growth forecast upward to 5.5% in January 2021, 0.3 percentage points higher than its forecast made in October 2020 (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real GDP growth forecasts by the International Monetary Fund made in January 2021 and October 2020. Against this backdrop, market optimism strengthened, and share prices of cyclical industries that typically benefit from economic recovery rose, driving global share prices and valuations to new highs at the beginning of 2021 (Chart 2.2). Chart 2.2 The 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratios of major stock indices. However, while financial markets performed strongly, the macroeconomic situation remained full of challenges, and the disconnect between the two could lead to volatility in asset markets amid multiple risks. First, the prospect of the pandemic being brought under control depends on whether vaccines can be widely distributed, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, the overall global vaccination rate remained low (Chart 2.3). Although there are global mechanisms (such as COVAX) to promote a more equitable distribution of vaccines, the problem of low vaccination rates in lower-income emerging market economies is expected to be more severe due to limited vaccine supply. If the pandemic is not brought under control as hoped, various places may need to continue social distancing measures and other restrictions, thereby undermining the global recovery outlook. Chart 2.3 Proportion of the population having received at least one dose of vaccine in selected economies (as of 15 March 2021). Second, the rebound in financial markets is built upon sustained monetary and fiscal policy support, particularly the "lower for longer" monetary policy. However, there is a risk that support measures could be withdrawn faster than expected. For example, under the combined effects of supply bottlenecks, strong monetary and liquidity growth, and aggressive fiscal easing, inflation expectations in the US and Europe have already risen (Chart 2.4). If future inflation is stronger than expected, central banks may need to scale back their policy-easing, and inflation data exceeding expectations could also lead to greater volatility in financial markets. Chart 2.4 The 5-year/5-year inflation-linked swap rates in the US and the Euro area. Third, there is significant uncertainty surrounding future US-China relations. The wave of US-China "decoupling", particularly in the financial and technology sectors, has intensified since the outbreak of the pandemic. Given the increasingly hardline attitude of both the Democratic and Republican parties in the US towards Mainland China, this trend may not be reversed under the Biden administration. Any unexpected escalation of US-China tensions could trigger turbulence in financial markets in the future. Looking ahead, policymakers will need to grapple with the difficult question of whether and when to withdraw pandemic support measures. While withdrawing such measures prematurely could jeopardise the economic recovery and create a "cliff effect", these measures are costly in the long run, including imposing a fiscal burden and delaying the necessary reallocation of resources after the pandemic—for example, allowing "zombie enterprises" whose business models are no longer viable to survive under continued government support. In addition, policymakers must also address the many problems left behind by the pandemic. First, due to declining corporate revenues and surging government expenditure, global debt levels rose sharply in 2020 (Chart 2.5). Although the surge in debt may not pose an imminent problem given that global interest rates are currently at extremely low levels, the continued accumulation of debt in the public and private sectors could raise market concerns about fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Chart 2.5 The ratio of global debt to GDP. Another lingering problem concerns the potential long-term economic losses or long-lasting scarring that the pandemic may cause. For example, elevated uncertainty could cause businesses to reduce investment, while workers plagued by long-term unemployment may permanently exit the labour market, resulting in a significant waste of human resources. In East Asia, real GDP growth stabilised in the second half of 2020 after plunging in the second quarter (Chart 2.6). The momentum of the economic recovery came mainly from a rebound in exports, with export demand for electronics and technology equipment being the strongest. At the same time, the hardest-hit service industries (such as tourism and consumer services that require face-to-face contact with customers) continued to struggle. As a result, the less-developed economies in the region may achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, and uneven vaccination among the various economies could prolong border closures and delay the recovery of tourism-related industries. Second, since investors' optimism is largely driven by the vaccine rollout, if the progress or effectiveness of vaccination falls far short of expectations, the current capital inflows and the rebound in financial asset prices could come to an end. With the novel coronavirus successfully brought under control and consumption gradually recovering, the Mainland economy rebounded rapidly in the second half of 2020. At the same time, benefiting from strong demand for pandemic-related products (such as medical supplies and high-tech products), exports also maintained growth (Chart 2.8). As the COVID-19 pandemic raged, inbound tourism rapidly fell into slump, and there are market concerns that this crisis could have scarring effects on the future recovery of the labour market. Against this backdrop, this Box empirically analyses the impact of the boom in inbound tourism on Hong Kong's labour market, so as to explore the potential impact of the current tourism slump. Since 2000, inbound tourism has experienced sharp ups and downs (Chart B2.1). Specifically, visitor arrivals declined during the SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) outbreak in 2003. Following the launch of the Individual Visit Scheme (IVS) in July of that year, the number of visitors began to surge. Under the initial IVS, Mainland residents could apply to visit Hong Kong on an individual basis one to two times a year, staying no more than seven days per visit. The IVS was expanded from April 2009, allowing eligible residents holding Shenzhen household registration to apply for a multiple-entry Individual Visit Endorsement (multiple-entry permit). Since then, the number of Mainland visitors has increased substantially. Driven by new cross-boundary infrastructure connecting to Mainland China, visitor arrivals reached an all-time high level around late 2018 to early 2019. Subsequent local social events halved the number of visitors in the second half of 2019, and amid the COVID-19 pandemic, inbound tourism has been at a standstill since late January 2020.  Chart B2.1 Visitor arrivals and related policies  We take the tourism boom brought about by the IVS as an example to examine the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and earnings. We regard the IVS launched in 2003 as akin to a random economic shock, as it was nearly exogenous in timing and could not be anticipated by local residents. Our main analytical data come from population data in the Hong Kong Population Census or By-census. Specifically, we use the 5% samples from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011 and 2016 Population Censuses or By-censuses. In addition, we define tourism-related industries as the food, retail, accommodation and transportation sectors. First, we adopt the difference-in-differences approach as our analytical framework, comparing the difference in employment outcomes before and after the implementation of the IVS between younger workers (aged 20–40) in the treatment group and older workers (aged 41–65) in the comparison group. We assign the younger group to the treatment group because they are still in the early stages of their careers and can more flexibly make significant changes to their employment choices in response to the exogenous growth in inbound tourism. As the impact of the tourism boom brought about by the IVS on the labour market may change over time, we also adopt the event study approach to identify time-varying effects. Our empirical findings show that, compared with the older group, younger workers (especially women and those with only secondary education) were more likely to enter tourism-related industries after the implementation of the IVS. In particular, the impact of the IVS on the probability of young women working in tourism-related industries was especially significant and persistent, remaining at close to 5 percentage points from 2006 onwards (in terms of the average difference in the probability of entry relative to the older group) (Chart B2.2). We also use a similar approach to compare the earnings of those working in tourism-related industries (treatment group) with those in non-tourism-related industries (comparison group). The estimation results show that, after the implementation of the IVS, the earnings growth of workers in tourism-related industries was higher than that of employees in non-tourism-related industries. Moreover, compared with similar employees in other industries, female workers and lower-educated workers in tourism-related industries saw higher earnings gains that trended upward (3–20 percentage points) (Chart B2.3).  Chart B2.2 Impact of the IVS on female employment Chart B2.3 Impact of the IVS on the earnings of women and lower-educated workers  The above results are broadly consistent with international experience, revealing that tourism is an important source of employment, especially for young people, women and lower-educated workers. As for Hong Kong, our findings are also consistent with previous analyses, namely that the strong growth in inbound tourism increased market demand for lower-skilled workers and improved the resilience of the lower-skilled segment of the labour market. As inbound tourism falls from boom to trough, these worker groups may be more affected and warrant close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate continued to trade close to the strong-side CUs, which were triggered multiple times during September to October 2020. The strong Hong Kong dollar demand was mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including that from buoyant IPO activities, as well as southbound fund flows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. As the Aggregate Balance increased to over HK$450 billion, HIBORs declined across the board. Although uncertainties related to the development of the COVID-19 pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and the continued tensions in Sino-US relations may intensify fund flow volatility, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign reserves and a sound banking system, and is capable of withstanding the pressures brought by fund flow volatility. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate traded close to the strong-side CUs, mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including that from buoyant IPO activities, as well as southbound fund flows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.1). Although part of the funds raised from IPOs was remitted out, owing to improved market sentiment in the local stock market and market expectations of rising funding demand near the year-end, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate traded within a narrow range of 7.7505 to 7.7544 in November and December. With fundraising activities remaining active in the first two months of 2021 (Chart 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar closed at 7.7568 against the US dollar on 26 February 2021. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading remained smooth and orderly. During the review period, the strong-side CUs were triggered multiple times, leading to an increase in the Aggregate Balance and reflecting substantial fund inflows into the Hong Kong dollar. From September to October 2020, the strong-side CUs were triggered 47 times. In accordance with the design of the LERS, the HKMA sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, increasing the Aggregate Balance from HK$193.1 billion at the end of August to HK$457.5 billion at the end of February (Chart 4.3). The strong-side CUs were triggered a total of 85 times throughout 2020, with cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. From a cross-border perspective, total deposits increased, showing no sign of any large-scale outflow of funds from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments figures showed that non-residents' direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, without any indication of abnormal fund flows. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index generally declined in line with the softening of the US dollar against major currencies (Chart 4.4). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index, the movement of the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index broadly tracked that of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.4 Nominal and real effective exchange rates. Looking ahead, uncertainties related to the development of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and the continued tensions in Sino-US relations may intensify fund flow volatility. As an international financial centre, Hong Kong hosts various fundraising activities (such as IPO fundraising), resulting in substantial fund inflows into and outflows from Hong Kong. On the one hand, the relevant fundraising activities can attract international investors to move funds to Hong Kong. On the other hand, funds raised by listed corporates may subsequently be transferred out of Hong Kong as needed for their business. Hong Kong possesses ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system, and is capable of withstanding fund flow volatility without affecting financial stability. Amid continued fund inflows into the Hong Kong dollar, the local monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. In the eight months since the end of June 2020, the HKD Monetary Base increased by 20.8% (Chart 4.5). By component, the increase in the Monetary Base during this period reflected the increase in the Aggregate Balance arising from the multiple triggering of the strong-side CUs. On the other hand, other components, including Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base. During the review period, large-scale IPO activities increased Hong Kong dollar deposits derived from IPO subscription loans, so Hong Kong dollar broad money (Hong Kong dollar M3) and its Hong Kong dollar deposit component rose significantly from July to October 2020 and in January 2021 (Chart 4.6). As IPO activities concluded and customers repaid IPO subscription loans, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money returned to normal levels at the end of 2020. Entering January 2021, Hong Kong dollar M3 again increased substantially, mainly driven by large-scale IPO activities at the end of January. Overall, in the seven months since the end of June, Hong Kong dollar M3 grew by 21.7%, but excluding the impact of the IPO activities at the end of January, Hong Kong dollar M3 grew moderately by 9.1%. According to the analysis of counterpart assets, excluding IPO subscription loans, the growth in Hong Kong dollar M3 was mainly attributable to the increase in the Monetary Base driven by the triggering of the strong-side CUs (Chart 4.7). As a major component of Hong Kong dollar M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose by 22.9% over the same period, but excluding the impact of the IPO activities at the end of January, Hong Kong dollar deposits grew moderately by 9.1%. Although Hong Kong dollar time deposits recorded a decline due to low deposit interest rates, this was fully offset by the rapid growth in demand and savings deposits driven in part by investment demand. Total foreign currency deposits grew steadily by 3.6% in the seven months since the end of June. US dollar deposits edged down by 0.3%, partly reflecting the weak US dollar, while other foreign currency deposits grew strongly by 15.5% over the same period, mainly reflecting the increase in renminbi deposits. Overall, as IPO activities caused short-term fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar deposits, total deposits with AIs rose significantly by 13.2% during the review period (Chart 4.6). Excluding the IPO activities at the end of January, total deposits grew moderately by 6.4%. On the other hand, the Best Lending Rates of retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Under the LERS, HKD interest rates are influenced by their USD counterparts. Given the prolonged low US interest rates, HKD interest rates should continue to remain low, with occasional fluctuations driven by capital markets activities and seasonal liquidity demand. Faced with a highly uncertain macro-financial environment, the ample liquidity in the banking system should provide a sufficient buffer to maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. The exchange rates of the offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore renminbi (CNY) against the US dollar strengthened since the end of May (Chart 4.10), broadly reflecting Mainland China's better economic outlook relative to the rest of the world, as well as the weak US dollar. With FTSE Russell announcing at the end of September the inclusion of Mainland government bonds in the World Government Bond Index, investment demand further supported the strengthening of the renminbi. The 3-month CNH HIBOR followed onshore renminbi interest rates and declined in late December, and then rose again in late January, partly owing to tighter onshore liquidity and seasonal factors. Compared with the end of June 2020, the balance of RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew at a faster pace, reaching RMB826.3 billion at the end of January 2021, an increase of 21.9% (Chart 4.12 and Table 4.A). Amid the persistent economic recession caused by the recurrence of the novel coronavirus pandemic, and under the influence of a prolonged low interest rate environment, the profitability of Hong Kong's retail banks declined further in the second half of 2020, with asset quality also deteriorating slightly. Nevertheless, the Hong Kong banking sector remained sound, underpinned by its still-robust capital and liquidity positions. During the review period, in order to continue supporting the overall economy through difficult times, the HKMA decided to extend a number of relief measures. Looking ahead, although the roll-out of vaccines may raise hopes that the global pandemic can be brought under control and economic activities can resume, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. The aforementioned uncertainties, together with ongoing geopolitical tensions, will weigh on business activities and continue to pose challenges to the local banking sector. In particular, the pandemic will erode the repayment ability of corporates and households, so the banking sector should continue to closely monitor the impact of related downside risks on its asset quality. In the second half of 2020, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 38.5% compared with the same period in 2019. Correspondingly, the return on assets declined to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, down from 1.13% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.1). The net interest margin of retail banks narrowed from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 to 1.01% in the same period of 2020 (Chart 5.2), reducing net interest income and outweighing the slight increase in non-interest income, resulting in lower profitability. For the whole of 2020, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 29.4%, and the return on assets decreased from 1.19% in 2019 to 0.77%. Chart 5.1 Retail bank profitability. Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks. Largely due to substantial capital inflows driven by equity markets activity, Hong Kong dollar liquidity became more ample. HIBORs softened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. In particular, the 3-month HIBOR fell by 43 basis points in the second half to 0.35% at the end of 2020 (the blue line in Chart 5.3). The composite interest rate (an indicator measuring the average HKD funds cost of retail banks) followed a broadly similar trend, declining significantly from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.28% at the end of 2020 (the green line in Chart 5.3). The decline in the composite interest rate mainly reflected the lower interbank funding costs and the lowering of time deposit rates by some major retail banks. Chart 5.3 Interest rates. From a broader perspective, the average overall HKD and US dollar funding costs of Hong Kong's licensed banks fell moderately by 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (the red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 HKD and US dollar funding costs and maturities of licensed banks. Looking ahead, as the global low interest rate environment is likely to persist and continue to weigh on banks' net interest margin performance, the profitability outlook of the banking sector will remain challenging. In addition, although breakthroughs in vaccine development have strengthened market optimism about the global economic outlook, given the considerable uncertainties surrounding the distribution and efficacy of vaccines, the trajectory of economic recovery remains highly uncertain. The aforementioned risk factors will continue to affect the loan quality and profitability of the banking sector in the near term. The capital position of the Hong Kong banking sector remained sound and well above minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions stood at 20.7% at the end of December 2020, higher than the international minimum requirement of 8% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio during the period was 18.7%, of which 16.7% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions was maintained at a sound level of 8.2% at the end of December 2020, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.5 Capital position of locally incorporated authorized institutions. Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions. As measured by the "Liquidity Coverage Ratio" requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions was 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum of 100%. During the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions was 57.9%, also well above the statutory minimum of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio. The latest ratio figures under the "Net Stable Funding Ratio" requirement also indicate that the funding position of authorized institutions was stable. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions and the average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions were maintained at high levels of 138.6% and 139.5% respectively in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.8), well above their statutory minimums of 100% and 75% respectively. The ample liquidity and sound funding position of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector can withstand liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio. Customer deposits remained the main source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting a stable funding structure of the banking system. At the end of 2020, Customer deposits accounted for 56.1% of the total liabilities of all authorized institutions, broadly similar to the level six months earlier (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all authorized institutions. As total deposits of all authorized institutions increased in the second half of 2020 while total lending decreased over the same period, the average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions in all currencies fell from 76.0% at the end of June 2020 to 72.3% at the end of 2020 (Chart 5.10). The increase in total deposits largely reflected growth in both Hong Kong dollar deposits and foreign currency deposits. Correspondingly, as at the end of 2020, the average Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio and foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 83.5% and 61.0% respectively, compared with 86.4% and 65.5% respectively six months earlier. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions. The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained relatively low in the fourth quarter of 2020. Under a shock of a 200 basis point rise in HKD and USD interest rates, the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks could decline by an amount estimated to be equivalent to 1.41% of their total capital base at the end of December 2020 (Chart 5.11). Chart 5.11 Impact of HKD and USD counterparts interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks. Against the backdrop of the persistent economic recession caused by the recurrence of the pandemic and the tightening of social distancing measures, total loans and advances recorded a moderate decline in the second half of 2020. However, for the whole of 2020, total credit of the banking sector still recorded positive growth, although its growth rate slowed significantly from 6.7% in 2019 to 1.2%. On a half-yearly basis, after growing by 3.0% in the first half of 2020, the total loans and advances of all authorized institutions decreased by 1.8% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The decline in total lending was due to decreases in both domestic loans (including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade finance) and loans for use outside Hong Kong. In particular, total domestic loans edged down by 0.9% in the second half, while total loans for use outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.9%, compared with growth of 2.6% and 4.2% respectively in the preceding six months. Chart 5.12 Loan growth. Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans, after decreasing by 2.0% in the first half, remained broadly at the same level at the end of 2020 as at the end of June. Foreign currency loans, after growing substantially by 10.6% in the first half of 2020, decreased by 4.5% in the second half, partly reflecting a decline in US dollar loan demand as global liquidity conditions improved. The banking sector's outlook for short-term credit demand turned slightly more optimistic than six months earlier. The HKMA's Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook of December 2020 showed that the proportion of surveyed authorized institutions expecting loan demand to increase over the next three months rose to 37%, while the proportion expecting loan demand to decrease over the same period fell to 13% (Table 5.A). As the pandemic adversely affected the repayment ability of households and companies, banks' loan quality deteriorated slightly, but remained sound by historical and international standards. Moreover, the pace of deterioration in loan quality also slowed in the second half of 2020. The gross CLR of all authorized institutions rose moderately from 0.79% six months earlier to 0.9% at the end of 2020, while the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans of all authorized institutions rose from 0.49% at the end of June 2020 to 0.57% at the end of 2020. For retail banks, the gross CLR and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans rose to 0.82% and 0.48% respectively (Chart 5.13).

As 2022 began, global economic performance was sluggish, but inflationary pressures continued to intensify in various regions, especially the United States. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties, including the risk of a large-scale outbreak of the pandemic, and the possibility that if US inflation proves more persistent and broad-based than expected, the tightening of monetary policy may exceed expectations. If the US Federal Reserve tightens monetary policy substantially and leads to a tightening of global financing conditions, this would put pressure on the recovery of the more fragile emerging market economies. Recently, the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine may bring significant impacts on the global economy through trade and financial channels, and further complicate the outlook for global monetary policy. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened, but trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, and there was no significant sign of funds flowing out of the Hong Kong banking system. For the full year of 2021, the growth of total bank loans accelerated somewhat. On the other hand, the residential property market has softened since mid-2021. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may pose a threat to the sustained economic recovery, coupled with the possibility that the pace of US monetary policy normalisation may be faster than expected; these risk factors will pose challenges to banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of the relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The global economy began to slow in late 2021, with the weakness continuing into 2022, due to the spread of the highly contagious Omicron variant leading to increased restrictions on the movement of people globally, coupled with persistent supply bottlenecks putting pressure on production. At the same time, amid supply-demand imbalances and labour shortages, global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and have spread to a broad range of goods and services in major advanced economies, especially the United States. Recently, with the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine, the sharp rise in commodity prices could further exacerbate the threat of global inflation, while heightened financial market volatility may lead to a less-than-ideal tightening of global financing conditions, further complicating the outlook for global monetary policy. Looking ahead, there are significant uncertainties in the global economic outlook. In the short term, if there is a large-scale outbreak of the pandemic, the re-imposition of lockdown measures and the renewed worsening of supply bottlenecks cannot be ruled out. In the United States, as the risk of inflation being more persistent and broad-based than expected grows, the Federal Reserve's stance has turned hawkish, accelerating the timeline for tapering asset purchases and raising interest rates, and beginning to discuss shrinking its balance sheet. If the Federal Reserve needs to tighten monetary policy substantially, global financing conditions may also tighten, leading to a deterioration in borrowers' debt repayment abilities, while disorderly capital outflows would put pressure on the recovery of the relatively fragile emerging market economies. Recently, the Russia-Ukraine conflict may pose the risk of persistently rising global commodity prices, aggravating shortages in the supply of industrial goods and increasing financial market volatility. Heightened market volatility could also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risk. Feature Article 1 discusses whether swing pricing (a tool for open-ended funds to manage their liquidity) can reduce the liquidity risk of these funds during periods of market stress, and discusses the potential limitations of this tool. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, but the recovery momentum slowed for a time as some Southeast Asian economies re-imposed strict pandemic control measures in the third quarter, while the region's technology-product-exporting economies (South Korea and Singapore) continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products. Although the market generally expects a broad-based recovery in emerging Asia in 2022, the region's short-term economic outlook is facing multiple headwinds. First, the new variant remains a concern, especially for economies in the region with lower vaccination rates and tight public health resources. Second, the acceleration of policy normalisation by the Federal Reserve could trigger capital outflows from the region and aggravate currency depreciation pressures; and for economies in the region that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policy to support economic recovery, the trade-off between curbing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity will become more difficult. Third, the slowdown in major economies, coupled with the possibility that demand may shift from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, will put pressure on the trade growth outlook. Fourth, the rise in the prices of various commodities triggered by the Russia-Ukraine conflict will be transmitted to inflation in the region while simultaneously dampening consumption. Coupled with the increased global economic uncertainty, the monetary policy normalisation decisions of the region's central banks will become more complex. For some economies in the region with weaker growth momentum and inflation more sensitive to energy prices, their central banks will face particularly difficult trade-offs. In the long run, in order to rebuild a sustainable and robust growth model, investors need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Feature Article 2 examines the sensitivity of equity returns to changes in climate risk, and how such sensitivity is affected by firms' environmental performance. Mainland China's economic growth slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power rationing measures, and property market tightening measures. Looking ahead, due to the persistent weakness in the housing market and the outbreak of the Omicron variant, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressures in the short term. Therefore, the Mainland authorities have made stabilising growth the top priority for this year and have rolled out a series of fiscal and monetary support measures. In the second half of 2021, both the total amount of onshore bond defaults and the onshore bond defaults of state-owned enterprises (SOEs) decreased. Feature Article 3 discusses whether the pricing of SOE bonds has improved in recent years. The overall risk in the banking sector remains manageable, as Mainland banks (especially systemically important banks) have limited exposure to loans to developers, with low non-performing loan (NPL) ratios and high provision coverage ratios. Hong Kong's economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, but at a slower pace than in the first half. As goods exports and private consumption benefited from the sustained global economic recovery, the improvement in local labour market conditions, and the government's launch of the consumption voucher scheme, seasonally adjusted real GDP grew moderately. On a year-on-year basis, the economy grew by 5.1% in the second half of 2021, compared with 7.8% in the first half. For the full year of 2021, the economy grew by 6.4%, marking the first full-year positive growth since 2019. As 2022 began, a new wave of local infections and the resulting tightening of social distancing measures put pressure on Hong Kong's economic activity. The government rolled out the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional counter-cyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the "100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme" and the various guarantee products under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme will be enhanced, with the maximum loan amount raised and the application period and repayment period extended. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, has also extended the "Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme" to the end of October 2022. The scheme also provides borrowers with a one-year partial principal repayment option, which is also applicable to loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. Hong Kong's economy is expected to continue recovering for the full year of 2022, but the pace of growth will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting the slowdown in global growth amid the ongoing pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong's goods exports will continue to benefit from the global economic expansion. The various works and infrastructure projects being promoted by the government will also provide support for the economy. The government forecasts real GDP growth of between 2.0% and 3.5% in 2022, while the average growth forecast of international organisations and private-sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are affected by a number of uncertainties and risks discussed in the previous sections, particularly the pandemic and the pace of US monetary policy normalisation. As the economy recovered, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% by year-end. Total employment rebounded but remained below pre-pandemic levels. In early 2022, official data showed that labour market pressures re-emerged amid a new wave of local infections. In addition, the decline in the number of online job advertisements also reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. The new wave of local infections and the tightening of anti-epidemic measures will put some pressure on the local labour market in the short term, especially in industries involving face-to-face contact. In the longer term, labour market conditions will depend on the development of the local pandemic and the pace of the local economic recovery. Local inflationary pressures have broadly increased in recent months but remained mild. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying consumer price inflation rate edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022. The three-month-on-three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also picked up in recent months, partly due to the rise in prices of dining out and some energy-related items. Looking ahead, with rising import prices and pandemic-induced disruptions to logistics, local inflation is expected to edge up slightly in the short term. However, soft rents and mild local labour cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. Market consensus forecasts headline inflation of 2.4% in 2022, while the government forecasts headline inflation of 2.1% and underlying inflation of 2.0% in 2022. Since September 2021, amid risk-averse sentiment in the local stock market, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually softened against the US dollar. Although the Hong Kong dollar rebounded slightly in October 2021, its upward momentum subsequently faded, mainly due to weak southbound net buying through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect, as well as market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen as the Federal Reserve normalises its monetary policy. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar traded on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone bounded by the CUs for most of the time, with trading continuing to be smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no significant sign of funds flowing out of the Hong Kong banking system. As virus variants (Delta and Omicron) spread rapidly around the world, coupled with persistent production bottlenecks, the global economy slowed markedly in late 2021, and growth momentum remained weak entering 2022. Global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and had already spread to a broad range of goods and services in major advanced economies (particularly the US). Rising inflation concerns prompted the Federal Reserve to shift its monetary policy stance towards a more hawkish position, heightening the risk that a premature tightening of global financing conditions could weigh on currently elevated asset valuation, and would also be unfavourable to emerging markets where recovery generally remains lagging. Recently, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine has pushed up energy prices and other commodity prices, and triggered financial market volatility, exacerbating some of the aforementioned risks. In emerging Asia, despite the spread of the Delta variant within the region, the economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, with the region's major technology product exporting economies continuing to perform better than other economies. While the current Omicron variant is not expected to seriously hamper the region's economic recovery, any uncertainty related to new virus variants will continue to cast a shadow over the region's economic outlook. In addition, the normalisation of Federal Reserve policy may also trigger an adjustment in the region's asset prices, while slowing economic growth in major economies may also weigh on the growth of the region's exports of goods. On one hand, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine has led to rising commodity prices and increased inflation risks; on the other hand, it will dampen consumption and increase global economic uncertainty, which will make decisions on the normalisation of monetary policy by the region's central banks more complicated. Mainland China's economic growth slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power rationing, and tightening measures in the housing market. Looking ahead, Mainland China's economy may continue to face downward pressures brought about by a cooling housing market and the outbreak of the Omicron variant. In view of this, the government has designated stabilising growth as its top priority this year, and macroeconomic policy will also provide greater support. The global economic recovery slowed markedly in the final quarter of 2021, as the highly contagious Omicron variant overlapped with the spread of the Delta variant, triggering a new wave of infections and leading to the tightening of restrictions on people's movement around the world. In addition, supply chain issues (such as shipping bottlenecks and shortages of key production raw materials such as semiconductors) continued to weigh on production. Entering 2022, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in January forecast that global GDP growth would slow from 5.9% in 2021 to 4.4% in 2022, reflecting the continued drag from the pandemic and supply constraints, reduced policy support in the US and other major advanced economies, as well as slowing growth drivers in Mainland China offsetting the expected growth rebound in the rest of Asia (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 International Monetary Fund's real GDP growth forecast. Alongside the slowdown in global economic growth, inflationary pressures also continued to increase during the review period. Core inflation (excluding food and energy prices) rose significantly in major advanced economies, particularly the US, which had adopted larger-scale policy stimulus since the pandemic. Amid supply bottlenecks, unleashed pent-up demand and labour shortages, inflationary pressures had spread to a broad range of goods and services (Chart 2.2). In addition, the recent military conflict between Russia and Ukraine has pushed up the prices of various commodities, which may intensify already elevated global inflationary pressures. Chart 2.2 Core CPI inflation rates for selected economies. (1) The latest data for the US, UK and Euro area are for January 2022, while the rest are for December 2021. (2) "Asian advanced economies" include Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong and Singapore. (3) "Asian emerging market economies" include Mainland China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties with pronounced downside risks, and will depend on the development of the pandemic and related supply chain disruptions, how the impact of geopolitical tensions on global trade, inflation and financial market sentiment evolves, and the policy response of major central banks to inflation. On the pandemic front, most governments have so far adopted targeted measures in response to the recent surge in Omicron cases, focusing on restricting high-risk activities, encouraging remote work and promoting vaccination. Compared with previous lockdown policies, these more relaxed measures should help reduce supply chain disruptions, which have shown initial signs of improvement since late 2021 (Chart 2.3). However, in the event of a large-scale outbreak, it cannot be ruled out that lockdown measures may be reimposed, subsequently causing supply bottlenecks to worsen once again. Chart 2.3 Purchasing Managers' Index – sub-index of suppliers' delivery times. Should the pandemic remain under control, supply bottlenecks are expected to gradually improve, providing some relief to goods inflation. However, several developments may make the current elevated global inflation more persistent than expected, including the risk that the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine and sanctions on energy imports from Russia push up commodity prices, the lagged reflection of rising production costs in final selling prices, the possibility that the earlier surge in global residential property prices may drive up subsequent rents, the upside risk to wage growth from tight labour markets, and rising inflation expectations. In particular, given that US inflation recorded the largest increase in decades, the Federal Reserve shifted to a more hawkish policy stance at the Federal Open Markets Committee meeting in December 2021, no longer characterising high inflation as "transitory", and doubling the pace of asset purchase tapering from US$15 billion per month to US$30 billion, with a view to ending the asset purchase programme by March 2022 and beginning discussions on shrinking its balance sheet. Indeed, recent market pricing suggests that the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates multiple times in 2022. In contrast, given the Euro area's closer trade and financial ties with Russia and Ukraine, the ECB may face more significant policy trade-offs. Against this backdrop, coupled with global debt levels and asset valuation remaining persistently elevated under prolonged policy easing, should inflationary pressures persist and require the Fed to tighten policy faster than expected, it may leave borrowers' debt repayment abilities facing a risk of deterioration and trigger financial market volatility. Recently, as geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe have escalated, risk aversion in financial markets has increased, and signs of US dollar shortages have emerged, including a widening of cross-currency swap spreads. Amid a premature tightening of global financing conditions, emerging market economies with weaker fundamentals that are still affected by the pandemic may be vulnerable to renewed growth slowdowns, currency depreciation and capital outflow pressures. Increased market volatility may also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risk. Box 1 discusses whether swing pricing (a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds) can reduce the liquidity risk of these funds during periods of market stress, and discusses the potential limitations of this tool. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, but the spread of the Delta variant weakened growth momentum in the third quarter, particularly in some Southeast Asian economies (Chart 2.4). At the same time, as major technology product exporters in the region, South Korea and Singapore continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products, which further widened the unevenness of the recovery across the region. In addition, inflationary pressures in several emerging Asian economies remained mild. Chart 2.4 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index. Markets generally expect a broad-based recovery in Asian emerging markets in 2022, but the region's near-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds: First, although the Omicron variant has spread within the region since late 2021, its economic impact has been milder than previous waves of infection; however, some economies in the region where the vaccination rate still lags and public health resources are relatively tight will continue to face the threat of new virus variants emerging. Second, the normalisation of Federal Reserve policy may trigger capital outflows and create currency depreciation pressures on the region's currencies. For economies in the region that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policy to support economic recovery, the trade-off between curbing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity will become more difficult. At the long end of the yield curve, given the historically high correlation between the two yields (Chart 2.5), the risk of a sudden surge in US long-term yields would also spread to long-term bond yields in emerging Asia, exacerbating the risk of adjustments in the region's asset markets. Chart 2.5 Correlation between Asian ten-year sovereign bond yields and the corresponding US Central Government bond yields. Third, the region's goods trade outlook faces uncertainties arising from a slowdown in major economies and the possibility that demand may shift from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, and these factors may weaken the region's export growth. Chart 2.6 US: Imports from emerging Asia and real GDP. Fourth, although the region's economies have relatively limited trade and financial ties with Russia and Ukraine, the rise in commodity prices triggered by the conflict will be transmitted to the region's inflation while simultaneously dampening consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, decisions on the normalisation of monetary policy by the region's central banks will become more complicated. Central banks in some of the region's economies with weaker growth momentum and inflation more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. The pandemic has also alerted the region's economies to the long-term need to rebuild more sustainable and resilient growth models to prepare for other risks such as climate change. To this end, investors need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Box 2 examines whether equity markets returns are affected by changes in climate risk, and how such sensitivity is influenced by corporate environmental performance. The COVID-19 pandemic caused a huge shock to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turmoil, some open-ended funds suffered large outflows (Chart B1.1), placing pressure on their ability to manage their liquidity. Chart B1.1 Outflows from some open-ended funds during the March 2020 episode. In addition to investors' liquidity needs, another reason for the large outflows may be that investors adopted a "first-mover advantage" by redeeming their funds early, thereby avoiding bearing the redemption costs that may surge under market stress conditions. To curb outflows caused by the first-mover advantage, some open-ended funds adopt swing pricing — an open-ended fund pricing rule that reduces investors' first-mover advantage. Although many open-ended funds used swing pricing during this episode, there has been no empirical study indicating whether swing pricing can effectively reduce outflows from open-ended funds. Against this backdrop, this box conducts an empirical study to understand whether swing pricing was able to reduce outflows from open-ended funds during the March 2020 episode, thereby reducing their liquidity risk. In addition, this box will also identify factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing during periods of market stress. Based on these assessments, we will make policy recommendations regarding financial stability. The first-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming ahead of other investors, thereby passing on the redemption costs to them. The first-mover advantage exists mainly in open-ended funds that adopt traditional pricing rules, whereby the subscription and redemption costs of the fund's investors (such as the transaction costs arising from portfolio adjustments) are reflected in the open-ended fund's price after the transaction is carried out. Driven by the sustained growth in exports of goods and private consumption, Hong Kong's economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, recording positive full-year growth for the first time since 2019. Entering 2022, a fresh wave of local COVID-19 infections and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures weighed on local economic activity. The economy is expected to remain on a recovery track for 2022 as a whole, though its strength and pace will be affected by uncertainties and risks such as the pandemic and the normalisation of US monetary policy. These adverse factors may also affect the labour market outlook following the notable improvement in 2021. Although local inflation may edge up slightly in the near term amid rising import prices, soft local rentals and labour cost should keep overall price pressures in check. Hong Kong's economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021. On a year-on-year comparison, real GDP grew further by 5.5% in the third quarter and by 4.8% in the fourth quarter (Table 3.A), but the pace of growth slowed compared with the first half of the year. For 2021 as a whole, real GDP grew by 6.4%, the first positive full-year growth since 2019. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contributions of the major expenditure component. On a quarter-on-quarter comparison, economic activity grew moderately by 0.6% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively (Chart 3.1). Domestically, improved labour market conditions, coupled with the Government's implementation of the Consumption Voucher Scheme, drove private consumption higher. However, aggregate investment spending fell back in the final quarter following two consecutive quarters of strong rebound. Externally, as the global economy continued to recover, Hong Kong's merchandise trade performance remained strong, while trade in services stayed weak, partly because inbound tourism remained stagnant (Chart 3.2). In net terms, external trade dragged on GDP in the third quarter but provided support to GDP growth in the fourth quarter. Chart 3.2 Export and import volume. A fresh wave of local COVID-19 infections and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures weighed on local economic activity in early 2022. The Government rolled out the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional counter-cyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the "100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme" and various guarantee products under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme will be enhanced, with the maximum loan amount raised and the application period and repayment period extended. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, will also extend the "Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme" to the end of October 2022. The scheme also offers borrowers a one-year partial principal repayment option, which is also applicable to loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. Hong Kong's economy is expected to continue to recover for 2022 as a whole, but the pace of growth will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting slower global economic growth amid the ongoing pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong's exports of goods will continue to benefit from the global economic expansion. The Government's promotion of various public works and infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of between 2.0% and 3.5% for 2022, while the average growth forecast by international organisations and private sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of Hong Kong's economic recovery are affected by the numerous uncertainties and risks described in the preceding chapters. In particular, recent pandemic developments, the accelerated pace of US monetary policy normalisation, and heightened geopolitical concerns (such as the Russia-Ukraine situation) have cast a shadow over the near-term economic outlook for Hong Kong and the world. On the other hand, an earlier-than-expected resumption of quarantine-free travel between Hong Kong and Mainland China could stimulate local economic growth. As the economy recovered, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% at the end of the year (Chart 3.3). Total employment in December 2021 also rebounded by 2.0% from its recent low in February 2021, though it remained below its pre-pandemic level. In early 2022, official data showed that labour market pressures re-emerged amid a fresh wave of local COVID-19 infections. In addition, the decline in the number of online job advertisements also reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. Looking ahead, a fresh wave of local COVID-19 infections and the tightening of COVID-19 restrictions will put some pressure on the local labour market in the near term (particularly in sectors involving face-to-face contact). Over the longer term, labour market conditions will depend on local pandemic developments and the pace of the local economic recovery. Chart 3.3 Labour market conditions. Local inflationary pressures have broadly increased in recent months but remained mild. On a year-on-year comparison, underlying consumer price inflation edged up slightly to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022 (Chart 3.4). The three-month-on-three-month annualised underlying inflation, which reflects inflation momentum, also picked up in recent months. Specifically, as local demand recovered and external prices rose (Chart 3.5), the prices of meals out and some energy-related items increased at a faster pace. At the same time, the housing rental component of the CCPI continued to decline broadly, thereby restraining overall inflation momentum (Chart 3.6). Although real unit labour costs remained soft, they rose slightly in recent quarters, partly due to an improvement in real average wages (Chart 3.7). Chart 3.4 Various measures reflecting consumer price inflation. Chart 3.5 Hong Kong's import prices. Chart 3.6 CCPI rental component and market rentals. Chart 3.7 Unit labour costs. Looking ahead, with rising import prices and pandemic-induced logistics disruptions, local inflation is expected to edge up slightly in the near term. However, soft rentals and mild local labour cost pressures should keep overall price pressures in check. Market consensus forecasts point to headline inflation reaching 2.4% for 2022, while the Government forecasts headline inflation of 2.1% and underlying inflation of 2.0% for 2022.

Amid risk-averse sentiment in the local stock market and concerns over the normalisation of US monetary policy, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened during the review period. As HKD liquidity remained ample, HIBORs continued to stay at low levels. Overall, trading in the Hong Kong dollar foreign exchange and money markets remained smooth and orderly. Looking ahead, although uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, the pandemic and escalating geopolitical tensions could intensify fund flow volatility, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system, giving it the capacity to withstand the shocks brought about by fund flow volatility. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar traded on the strong side of the CUs for most of the time, and trading remained smooth and orderly. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually softened against the US dollar amid risk-averse sentiment in the local stock market (Chart 4.1). Although improved market sentiment led to a mild rebound in the Hong Kong dollar in October 2021, its upward momentum subsequently faded, mainly due to weak southbound net buying through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.2), as well as market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen as the US Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook turned more hawkish. During the review period, new share fundraising activities continued to lend support to the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.3). Total deposits grew modestly during the review period, with no significant signs of funds flowing out of the Hong Kong banking system. At the same time, the latest balance of payments figures show that non-residents' direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the second half of 2021, with no signs of abnormal cross-border fund flows. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate. Chart 4.2 Southbound net buying through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. Chart 4.3 Equity funds raised on the Hong Kong Exchanges (HKEX). Although the US dollar strengthened during the review period, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index remained stable as the renminbi appreciated against the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.4). Given the small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index broadly tracked the movement of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.4 Nominal and real effective exchange rates. Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, pandemic developments and escalating geopolitical tensions could intensify fund flow volatility. As US dollar interest rates rise, under the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS), outflows of HKD funds (the pace and scale of which will depend on prevailing market conditions) could lead to a weakening of the Hong Kong dollar and trigger the weak-side CU. Hong Kong also possesses ample foreign reserves and a sound banking system, giving it the capacity to withstand fund flow volatility without affecting financial stability. During the review period, monetary conditions in Hong Kong remained accommodative. The HKD Monetary Base rose by 1.4% over the eight months since the end of June 2021, mainly driven by an increase in Certificates of Indebtedness. Reflecting additional issuance of paper to meet banks' sustained demand for Exchange Fund Bills amid ample liquidity in the banking system, Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased by HK$119.7 billion to HK$1,188.7 billion during the review period, with the Aggregate Balance (before discount window activities) correspondingly decreasing by HK$119.9 billion to HK$337.6 billion (Chart 4.5). Meanwhile, government-issued banknotes and coins remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes. Over the six months since the end of July 2021, total deposits with authorized institutions grew modestly by 4.5%, while Hong Kong dollar deposits rose slightly by 0.3%. However, it should be noted that monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand, as well as business- and investment-related activities), so it is advisable to observe longer-term trends. For the whole of 2021, total deposits and Hong Kong dollar deposits grew by 4.6% and 1.4% respectively. Chart 4.6 Deposits with authorized institutions by currency. Overall, trading in Hong Kong's interbank market remained smooth and orderly. As liquidity in the banking system was ample, HIBORs continued to stay at low levels despite market concerns over US monetary policy tightening (Chart 4.7). Partly reflecting market expectations of rising funding demand towards year-end, HIBORs edged up slightly in December 2021. The average lending rate for new mortgages rose slightly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. On the other hand, the Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Looking ahead, ample liquidity in the banking system can provide a sufficient buffer in the event of large-scale capital market activities or volatility in financial markets. Chart 4.7 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank interest rates. During the review period, the offshore renminbi interbank market continued to function normally. Affected by seasonal liquidity demand towards year-end, the overnight CNH HIBOR experienced slight fluctuations in late December 2021, while the 3-month CNH HIBOR remained relatively stable, hovering around 3% throughout the review period (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Overnight and 3-month CNH HIBOR fixings. In the second half of 2021, Hong Kong's CNH liquidity pool continued to grow steadily. Over the six months since the end of July 2021, the balance of RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew by 30.3%, reaching RMB1,113.5 billion at the end of January 2022 (Chart 4.9 and Table 4.A). Of this, RMB customer deposits increased by 33.5%, mainly driven by corporate fund inflows, offsetting a 48.0% decline in the balance of certificates of deposit. Chart 4.9 RMB deposits and certificates of deposit in Hong Kong. Over the six-month period since July 2021, although outstanding renminbi loans decreased by 10.2% to RMB167.6 billion, RMB trade settlements in Hong Kong continued to grow. Between the end of July 2021 and the end of January 2022, the transaction volume handled by local banks reached RMB3,763.0 billion (Chart 4.10), an increase of 18.3% from RMB3,181.0 billion in the same period last year. Hong Kong's large CNH liquidity pool continued to support a substantial volume of renminbi payment and financing transactions. For the whole of 2021, the average daily turnover of the RMB RTGS system rose from RMB1,191.5 billion in 2020 to RMB1,522.6 billion. Chart 4.10 RMB trade settlement remittances. Looking ahead, with the establishment of the two-way Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Bond Connect and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect, the continued opening up of the Mainland's capital account, increasing demand from international investors for renminbi assets, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the "Belt and Road" and "Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area" initiatives, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit. Major global stock markets continued to rise in the fourth quarter of 2021, but consolidated since January 2022 amid growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in developed economies and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict. Hong Kong's stock market remained sluggish in the fourth quarter of 2021, weighed down mainly by the sharp decline in technology stocks. Uncertainties over global risks and the development of the pandemic in Hong Kong caused the Hang Seng Index to fall to a nearly two-year low at the end of February. The residential property market has softened since mid-2021, partly affected by weakening asset market sentiment and a new local wave of the pandemic. Underpinned by robust capital and liquidity positions, the Hong Kong banking sector remained resilient. Banks should stay vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. Although US monetary policy normalisation may signal an improvement in banks' profitability, the near-term improvement may be partly offset by two factors. As such, it may take more time for the improvement in banks' net interest margin to materialise. In addition, the surge in Omicron variant cases may also bring uncertainties to the pace of economic recovery, thereby putting pressure on banks' asset quality and profitability.
