Climate change affects every aspect of life, and everyone has a responsibility to do their part in mitigating its impact. In this regard, the HKMA has devoted significant effort to advancing Hong Kong's climate goals and to enhancing global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following last year's inclusion of our first sustainability report as a chapter in the HKMA Annual Report 2021, this year we are publishing the Sustainability Report 2022 separately for the first time. I hope this report will give readers a deeper understanding of the HKMA's work strategies and priorities in strengthening the resilience of Hong Kong's banking system against climate change, building a green finance ecosystem, and putting into practice our role as a responsible investor and sustainable development institution. During the year, we made notable progress in advancing sustainable development work across the HKMA's major functions. In this report, you will learn about our specific measures and initiatives, with the following key highlights: Banks' daily operations face climate risk. As the banking regulator, the HKMA has taken concrete measures to strengthen banks' resilience against climate change. In 2022, we formulated a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into the supervisory process, and studied how to leverage the power of technology to help banks assess the impact of physical risks. In view of the growing number of green and sustainable products launched by banks, we also shared with the industry good practices on how to properly manage these products, in order to enhance banks' capabilities in climate risk management. The HKMA actively participates in various collaborative initiatives on addressing climate risk and promoting sustainable finance development. On the local front, we are working with other financial regulators through the "Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group" (Steering Group) to develop a local green classification framework; this framework will increase the transparency of financial markets and make green finance policies more consistent. At the international level, we are actively participating in various international organisations to help formulate policies for addressing climate change and to assess their impact on financial stability. Hong Kong is well positioned to meet Asia's demand for green and sustainable financing. Although 2022 was a rather challenging year for the global bond market, the issuance amount of green and sustainable debt in Hong Kong continued to record strong growth of 42%, with total issuance rising to US$80.5 billion, making it the largest centre in Asia for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuance². Relevant issuers included the Shenzhen Municipal People’s Government and the People’s Government of Hainan Province, whose issuances once again demonstrate Hong Kong's unique role in facilitating the flow of green and sustainable funds between the Mainland and international markets. The vibrant development of Hong Kong's green bond market is partly attributable to the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the Government in issuing green bonds worth nearly US$16 billion, with the proceeds raised allocated to more than 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, and energy efficiency and conservation. We also assisted the Government in achieving two "firsts": in May 2022, we helped the Government issue its first batch of Government Green Retail Bonds worth a total of HKD20 billion, which was the largest green retail bond issuance in the world at the time. In addition, we assisted the Government in issuing its first batch of tokenised green bonds in February 2023. This was the world's first tokenised green bond issued by a government, and this issuance marked our successful combination of strengths in the bond market, green and sustainable finance, and financial technology—a milestone achievement. Standards, data and talent are indispensable elements for driving the sound development of the climate finance ecosystem, and can only be established through the efforts and collaboration of different sectors. To this end, the HKMA works mainly through the Steering Group with other relevant government departments, regulators, academic institutions and the financial industry to develop the above elements. Apart from developing the local green classification framework mentioned above, the Steering Group also promotes skills training in the industry and improves Hong Kong's data resources through its "Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance". In addition, the Steering Group has made good progress in other areas such as mandatory disclosure of climate-related information and carbon market opportunities. In 2022, the HKMA further strengthened the exchange Fund's work on responsible investment, in particular by setting a target for the exchange Fund's investment portfolio to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. At the same time, we also enhanced our risk management work to improve the exchange Fund's climate resilience and risk-adjusted long-term returns. Furthermore, to fully capture the opportunities that climate change may bring, we are committed to promoting sustainable investment of the exchange Fund, seeking out investment opportunities that help support climate transition and mitigate climate change, so as to enhance the long-term returns of the portfolio. At the end of 2021, the weighted average carbon intensity of the exchange Fund's equity portfolio was 43% lower than the level in 2017. In fact, the exchange Fund's exposure to high-carbon assets has remained consistently lower than that of the overall market. In the future, we will continue to advance towards the net-zero emissions target by continuously strengthening the integration of environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors into the investment management process, actively exercising asset ownership, continuously collaborating with various stakeholders, and focusing on the decarbonisation and transition of the portfolio. At the HKMA, the "Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee", which I chair, is responsible for formulating the HKMA's sustainable development strategy. Our strategic direction is based on three pillars: the environment, staff, and social responsibility. On the environmental front, we are committed to promoting a green working environment and promoting a more environmentally friendly market to society; on the staff front, as a responsible and caring employer, we actively foster a healthy and inclusive working environment; and on the social responsibility front, we are committed to raising the public's level of financial literacy, promoting financial inclusion, and actively giving back to society. Compared with the level when we began tracking our carbon footprint in 2015, we achieved double-digit reductions in per-capita greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption and paper usage in 2022. More importantly, we have formulated a roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. In the short term, our goal is to completely eliminate Scope 1 emissions and, using 2015 as the baseline, to reduce Scope 2 emissions by 63% by 2030 or earlier. Addressing climate change and promoting sustainable development require the continuous efforts and collaboration of multiple parties. On this important global issue, we understand that we must take practical action and lead by example, working together with like-minded peers and international organisations. In the next section, we will outline the HKMA's short-term plans and work priorities in addressing climate change across its major functions. Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier is a formidable task, and we will spare no effort to reach this goal. We are confident that, with the joint efforts of all our colleagues, the financial industry and the general public, we can successfully address the climate challenges ahead. Eddie Yue, Chief Executive

In 2023, the HKMA will continue to promote the sustainable development of Hong Kong's financial industry, and fulfil its responsibilities as a responsible investor and a sustainable development institution. At the same time, through participating in international and regional organisations, the HKMA will also strive to promote the broad development and best practices of green and sustainable finance. As the regulator of the banking sector, we will endeavour to strengthen the climate resilience of the banking sector and further enhance our green finance ecosystem to support banks' green transition. Specifically, the HKMA will communicate with banks to understand their progress in implementing the supervisory requirements on climate risk management, incorporate climate factors into our supervisory review process, and revise the common assessment framework of the banking sector's "Green Baseline". At the same time, the HKMA will support banks' work in enhancing their climate resilience and risk management capabilities, such as exploring different measures and technological solutions to help banks identify, measure and monitor their climate risk exposures. The HKMA will also work with banks to launch the next round of climate risk stress-tested, as part of the regular supervisor-driven stress-tested exercise for 2023 to 2024. Participating banks will be required to assess their ability to cope with climate risk based on an optimised stress-tested framework; the framework covers various stress scenarios such as extreme climate and adverse economic environments. To promote the healthy development of banks in providing green and sustainable investment products, the HKMA will keep abreast of local and international market and regulatory developments, maintain communication with the industry, and provide guidance on the sales process in a timely manner. We will also conduct off-site thematic assessments to gain a comprehensive understanding of the green and sustainable investment products offered by banks. Meanwhile, to strengthen the building of a green finance ecosystem to support the green transition of the financial industry, the HKMA is planning to consult the industry on the structure and core elements for developing a local green classification framework. In terms of market development, to promote Hong Kong as a green and sustainable finance hub in the region, the HKMA will assist the Government in expanding the issuance scale of green bonds under the Government Green Bond Programme, and broaden the scope of the programme to cover sustainability bonds; at the same time, it will attract more green financing activities to take place in Hong Kong through the "Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme". The HKMA will also assist in implementing the Government-funded "Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme" to expand Hong Kong's talent pool in green finance. In addition, the HKMA will continue to encourage more Mainland local governments, institutions and enterprises to carry out green financing through Hong Kong, and explore the feasibility of combining the use of green finance and technology. On the other hand, we will continue to collaborate with other government departments and agencies through the "Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group" on cross-sectoral topics such as skills training and data, green taxonomy, climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, as well as carbon market opportunities. Through the Alliance for Green Commercial Banks, the HKMA will jointly launch various dedicated programmes with the International Finance Corporation in the Asian region, including conducting green finance research, providing unique market analysis, offering targeted professional training for banks, as well as providing practical guidance to assist banks in formulating roadmaps to develop green finance into a core business. Looking ahead, the alliance will work closely with its founding members, global partners and knowledge partners to launch a membership programme to expand the alliance's influence in the Asian region. At the same time, the alliance will also enhance the professional capabilities of industry practitioners, promote the sharing of green finance knowledge, and take the lead in launching projects in new areas. As a responsible investor, the HKMA has set a target for the Exchange Fund's investment portfolio to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050, as its commitment to participating in global climate response efforts and implementing the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. Looking ahead, the HKMA will continue to incorporate environmental, social and governance factors into its investment management process, strive to move towards the net-zero emissions target, and fully support global climate response efforts. As a responsible and sustainable institution, the HKMA cares about both its staff and the general public and surrounding environment. We have formulated a sustainability roadmap and set climate targets for our own operations, as our commitment to participating in global decarbonisation and climate response efforts. The HKMA will continue to prioritise reducing carbon emissions, and encourage staff to give their full support in conserving energy and reducing waste. In addition, we will provide further guidance to staff to incorporate sustainability principles into the procurement process. To achieve digital transformation and enhance operational agility, the HKMA will explore ways to modernise its internal systems and applications to further improve work efficiency, while minimising as far as possible the potential risks that may arise during the digital transformation process.

Climate change is a significant risk facing the financial system. The HKMA has been committed to strengthening Hong Kong's financial system to build a greener and more sustainable future, contributing to Hong Kong's climate goals as well as the global sustainable development agenda. Banks encounter the impacts of various sustainability and climate-related issues in their day-to-day business operations. To continue fulfilling their vital functions in the financial system and to channel more funding towards green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risk. As the regulator of the banking sector, the HKMA places particular emphasis on building banks' capabilities to respond to and manage climate risk, and on accelerating banks' efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economy. The HKMA also supports banks in enhancing their capabilities to detect environmental crimes, and participated in the recently published Hong Kong Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment, which covers areas such as environmental crimes and illegal wildlife trafficking. In 2022, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (the Basel Committee)¹ issued the Principles for the Effective Management and Supervision of Climate-related Financial Risks, and issued responses to frequently asked questions, clarifying how the existing Basel framework covers the aforementioned risks. In response to these international developments, the HKMA will continue its efforts to incorporate climate-related factors into the supervisory framework. Following the issuance of the Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-1 "Climate Risk Management" in 2021, the HKMA has also maintained communication with banks, exchanging views on expectations, progress and challenges regarding the implementation of the relevant supervisory requirements. To further strengthen the supervision of banks' climate risk management, the HKMA has formulated a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into the banking supervisory process, which was communicated to the banking sector in June. As part of implementing the two-year plan, the HKMA issued the revised Supervisory Policy Manual module SA-1 "Risk-based Supervisory Approach", and enhanced the CAMEL² rating system by incorporating climate risk into the risk-based supervisory process. At the same time, drawing on the experience gained from the 2021 pilot exercise, the HKMA refined the climate risk stress-tested scenarios and assessment framework. The HKMA has also formulated a plan to incorporate the next round of climate risk stress-tested exercises into the regulator-led periodic stress-tested exercises, so as to conduct a more comprehensive assessment of the banking sector's resilience under extreme climate scenarios. Under this two-year plan, the HKMA is also enhancing its green assessment framework for banks to reflect the latest developments on sustainability-related issues (including climate risk management and transition planning). At the same time, the HKMA is reviewing the supervisory review process used to assess and monitor banks' capital adequacy and to determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements, with the aim of encouraging banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks to address risks related to climate change and the transition to carbon neutrality. Given the growing popularity of banks issuing green and sustainable products, the HKMA conducted a thematic review, primarily examining banks' development and ongoing management of these products. The HKMA identified some good practices during the thematic review process and issued a circular in December to share them with the industry, enabling banks to progressively enhance their climate risk management capabilities. The application of technology can improve data availability and strengthen banks' capabilities to manage climate risk. The HKMA has begun developing a common platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risks on real estate. In addition, the HKMA, together with other central banks and regulators, completed a project under the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Network to explore how technological solutions can assist in conducting physical risk assessments. The HKMA also attaches great importance to promoting sustainable and world-leading anti-money laundering practices; this work employs advanced analytics and regulatory technology, complemented by fully automated regulatory data collection. Over the past 12 months, the HKMA has streamlined the anti-money laundering regulatory data collection process to reduce the manpower burden and paper usage of banks. To enhance transparency across financial markets and to bring greater consistency to green finance policies, the HKMA has collaborated with other financial regulators to establish a local green classification framework. The green classification framework, commonly known as a green taxonomy, classifies economic activities as green or sustainable, providing a reference for authorities and market participants to determine whether an activity or its related products are genuinely green or sustainable. To this end, the HKMA has maintained contact with the industry and other relevant stakeholders to explore in depth the features and challenges of the framework, and is preparing to make recommendations and conduct a consultation on the structure and core elements of the framework in the first half of 2023. The HKMA is keenly aware that climate change may pose potential risks to the financial system, and has therefore incorporated a broader range of climate factors and scenarios into its financial risk analysis and research to strengthen its ongoing monitoring work. The HKMA takes climate change into account in its ongoing monitoring of financial stability risks, and has incorporated analysis of climate-related risks into its various financial stability reports. Through active participation in the scenario design and analysis workstream under the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA helps to further enrich climate scenarios, enabling central banks and regulators to gain a clearer understanding of the macroeconomic and financial impacts of climate change. In terms of research work, the HKMA conducted a number of applied research projects in 2022, exploring in depth two major topics, namely greenwashing behaviour in corporate green bond markets³, and the role of disclosure in mitigating climate risk exposures⁴. The above research findings help to inform the formulation of policy and regulatory measures to address the impact of climate risk on financial stability. Locally, these studies help strengthen the HKMA's ongoing monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate risk on financial stability. Externally, the HKMA has shared its research findings with a wide range of stakeholders through various channels, including international central bank research conferences and the HKMA's Half-Yearly Monetary and Financial Stability Report. The HKMA's Liquidity Facilities Framework is a collateralised standby liquidity facilities arrangement that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. The HKMA is studying the incorporation of sustainability considerations when assessing eligible collateral under this framework. The HKMA actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risk and mainstreaming sustainable finance. Through this participation, the HKMA helps promote international and regional policy dialogue on addressing climate change and its impact on financial stability, and draws on the insights gained to help strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong's financial system.

To consolidate Hong Kong's position as a green and sustainable finance hub in the region, the HKMA has stepped up its work to enhance market awareness and participation, provide the necessary infrastructure and enablers, and support international initiatives to align with global standards. The Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), co-led by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), is responsible for coordinating the financial sector's responses to climate and environmental risks, accelerating the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supporting the Government's climate strategy1. The Steering Group's work is largely modelled on its strategic plan, which sets out six key focus areas and five action agendas to consolidate Hong Kong's financial ecosystem and jointly build a greener and more sustainable future (Figure 1). Strengthening climate-related financial risk management to consolidate Hong Kong's position as a global risk management centre; promoting the flow of climate-related information at all levels to facilitate risk management, capital allocation and investor protection; enhancing the relevant skills of industry practitioners and strengthening public attention and awareness; encouraging product innovation and research measures to channel funds towards green and sustainable projects; capturing the business opportunities brought by the Mainland and developing Hong Kong into the green finance centre of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (Greater Bay Area); and strengthening regional and international cooperation. Actions taken so far to advance the development of sustainable finance in Hong Kong: The Steering Group has made good progress since its establishment. The Steering Group's current work priorities include skills training and data collection under the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance (see below), a green taxonomy (see the chapter "Building a Sustainable Financial System" on page 9, section "Establishing a Green Classification Framework to Facilitate Green Financing"), climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Specifically, the Steering Group announced in March a preliminary feasibility assessment of the carbon market opportunities for Hong Kong, and will support Hong Kong's development into a carbon trading centre in the region, including developing an international high-quality voluntary carbon market and capturing the opportunities brought by cooperation in the Greater Bay Area. In December, the Steering Group announced a collaboration with CDP2 to enhance data availability in Hong Kong and strengthen sustainability reporting. As part of this collaboration, the two parties developed a climate and environmental risk questionnaire targeting unlisted companies and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which both facilitates companies in conducting sustainability reporting and assists financial institutions in collecting and analysing company-level data for use in risk assessment and related business decisions. This is an important step for the Steering Group in expanding the coverage of its data work to include small and medium-sized enterprises, a previously hard-to-reach yet important segment of the economy. The Steering Group established the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance in July 2021, which is responsible for coordinating the work of financial regulators, government departments, industry stakeholders and academic institutions in training and policy formulation, and for building resource and databases. In the first half of 2022, the Centre launched three repositories on data, training information and internship opportunities respectively, to help the financial sector and other sectors access data and learning resources related to green and sustainable finance. The resource repository provides data sources for assessing Hong Kong's physical risks. To help nurture talent in the industry, the Centre assisted the Government in December to launch the "Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme", which provides funding for practitioners, students and graduates participating in green and sustainable finance related training and skills enhancement. Other measures to promote skills training include launching the "Sustainable Finance Internship Initiative" to create more internship opportunities for students, and developing a new "Green and Sustainable Finance" module under the HKMA's "Enhanced Competency Framework for Banking Practitioners" for bank practitioners3. "Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme". The HKMA has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance in the region. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA launched the "Alliance for Green Commercial Banks"4, bringing together financial institutions, banking sector organisations, research institutions and innovative technology providers in the region to jointly develop a cooperation platform for green commercial banks. The Alliance aims to enable commercial banks and other financial institutions to fully realise their potential, develop green finance into a mainstream core business, and promote the participation of the financial system in global climate change-related activities. Its mode of operation is as follows: it provides financial institutions with a one-stop mutual learning platform to obtain the knowledge, tools and information needed to formulate their own green finance roadmaps and transform into credible green financial institutions; it brings together green finance leaders and connects green financial institutions in different emerging markets to promote communication and explore frontier issues; and it advances the global green finance agenda, opening up boundless green and climate-related investment opportunities. In June, five leading global financial institutions5 became founding members of the Alliance, and worked closely with the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA to encourage clients to adopt green strategies, promote best practices for green products and services, and unlock new business opportunities that help achieve the green economic transition. In addition, three global partners and one knowledge partner6 committed in 2022 to provide climate expertise in areas ranging from innovation and standardisation to academic research. Details of the Alliance and its membership structure are set out on the relevant webpage (English version): founding members, and the International Finance Corporation and the HKMA signing a memorandum of understanding. On the other hand, since March 2021, the Alliance has held 18 training events and roundtables, attracting more than 6,000 participants from around the world, including the Asia-Pacific region, Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Americas. In addition, in June 2022 the Alliance, together with the Hong Kong Institute for Monetary and Financial Research (the Institute)7, published its first frontier issues research report titled "Climate Risk: Definitions, Measurement, Current Practices and Regulation". The HKMA has been promoting green and sustainable debt issuance and building an ecosystem of related local professional services. The total amount of green and sustainable debt (including bonds and loans) issued in Hong Kong in 2022 reached US$80.5 billion, an increase of 42%. +42% green and sustainable debt issuance (US$80.5 billion). To demonstrate the Government's determination to combat climate change, promote green finance, and commit to developing Hong Kong into a more sustainable and liveable city, the Government launched the Government Green Bond Programme in 2018, with the HKMA assisting in the implementation of the related green bond issuances. To date, the Government has issued green institutional and retail bonds equivalent to nearly US$16 billion, with the proceeds allocated to more than 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency and energy conservation. To enhance the transparency and accountability arrangements of the Programme, the Government publishes an annual Green Bond Report, detailing the allocation of the proceeds raised from the green bonds and the expected environmental benefits. To allow members of the public to participate in Hong Kong's sustainable development through investment and share in the results it brings, the first batch of green Retail Bonds with a total value of HKD 20 billion was issued in May, receiving enthusiastic public support and becoming the largest green retail bonds issuance globally at the time. This issuance also expanded the range of green and sustainable finance products in Hong Kong and consolidated Hong Kong's position as a premier green finance hub in the region and internationally. The Government also continued its regular green institutional bond issuance work in the 2022-23 financial year, and in January 2023 issued green bonds equivalent to US$5.75 billion. This tri-currency issuance covered the US dollar, euro and renminbi, with tenors ranging from 2 to 30 years, continuing to provide an important benchmark for potential issuers in Hong Kong and the region. The issuance was widely welcomed by the global investment community and successfully attracted new investors who had not previously participated in the Government's past green bond issuances, reflecting investors' confidence in Hong Kong's long-term credit profile and economic fundamentals. In response to investor demand, the Government doubled the issuance size of the renminbi bonds to RMB10 billion. The share of international investors and Mainland investors participating in this issuance through the southbound trading of Bond Connect also increased, demonstrating Hong Kong's role as a premier offshore CNH business hub and further consolidating Hong Kong's leading position as an international financial centre. In February 2023, the HKMA also assisted the Government in issuing a tokenised institutional green bond, to test the use of distributed ledger technology for bond issuance and settlement. This was the world's first tokenised green bond issued by a government. The primary issuance was settled on a T+1 basis on a private blockchain network, and the subsequent processes (including coupon payments, secondary market trading and settlement, and redemption at maturity) were also digitalised. The experience of this Government issuance can serve as a reference for market participants interested in conducting similar bond issuances in the future. To provide the industry with credible and convenient market information, the HKMA continued to collaborate with the Climate Bonds Initiative and the International Capital Market Association to publish annual reports on the green debt market in Hong Kong and the region respectively. The International Capital Market Association's report showed that in 2022 Hong Kong became the largest hub in Asia for arranging the issuance of international green and sustainable bonds, with the total amount of bonds arranged through Hong Kong reaching US$27.8 billion, accounting for more than one-third of the regional total. Asia's largest arranging hub for international green and sustainable bonds: US$27.8 billion. Following its first issuance in 2021, the Shenzhen Municipal People's Government again issued RMB5 billion of offshore local Government Bond in Hong Kong in November 2022, including RMB2.6 billion of green and blue bonds8. In the same month, the People's Government of Hainan Province also issued RMB5 billion of offshore bonds in Hong Kong for the first time, including blue and sustainable bonds. The above bond issuance activities once again highlight Hong Kong's unique role in facilitating green and sustainable fund flows between the Mainland and the rest of the world, as well as its long-standing position as a premier fundraising platform in the region. The HKMA continued to promote and implement the "Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme" launched in 2021, and used the scheme to attract more relevant professional service providers (including financial institutions, green advisory firms and external review agencies) to establish and expand their business in Hong Kong. The scheme has been widely welcomed by the industry. As at the end of 2022, the scheme had covered the pre-issuance, post-issuance or both external review service expenses of more than 180 issuers of green and sustainable debt instruments, helping issuers ensure and demonstrate strict adherence to market best practices and international standards. From March, the scheme was enhanced by lowering the minimum loan amount threshold for applying for external review fee subsidies from HKD 200 million to HKD 100 million, helping smaller enterprises obtain green financing. Following the successful completion of the proof-of-concept for a tokenised retail green bond under Project Genesis in 2021, the HKMA collaborated again with the BIS Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre under Genesis 2.0 to explore the technical feasibility of digitalised carbon forwards (also known as mitigation outcome interests, or MOI), thereby enhancing the transparency, objectivity and green elements of the green bond market. The project was completed in October 2022, successfully developing two prototypes that use blockchain and other related technologies to track, deliver and transfer digitalised MOI.

As one of the world's largest asset owners and managers, the HKMA plays an important role in promoting the development of green and sustainable finance to support the global climate change agenda. The HKMA is also a pioneer in responsible investment, having taken the lead in investing in green and sustainable assets as early as 2015, requiring its external investment managers to adopt the Principles of Responsible Ownership issued by the Securities and Futures Commission, and integrating environmental, social and governance factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The HKMA invests prudently in accordance with the principle of "capital preservation first, then long-term value enhancement", believing that attaching importance to environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors can unlock long-term sustainable value for investments and mitigate related risks. Facing the increasingly severe challenges of climate change, the HKMA continues to advance on its responsible investment journey, including setting the "Net Zero 2050" target in 2022 and optimising its risk management strategies, thereby enhancing the resilience of the asset portfolio and striving for more favourable long-term risk-adjusted returns for the Exchange Fund. The HKMA also actively participates in building a green and sustainable finance ecosystem, partnering with like-minded investors and regulatory authorities to jointly promote responsible investment, and collaborating with international organisations to formulate ESG investment standards. The transparency of climate-related information plays a pivotal role in managing climate risk. To fulfil its commitment to support the Glasgow Declaration issued by the Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) at the 2021 United Nations Climate Change Conference and to green the global financial system, the HKMA makes climate-related disclosures for the Exchange Fund in accordance with the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) under the Financial Stability Board. a. FCLTGlobal — Focusing Capital on the Long Term; b. PRI — Principles for Responsible Investment; c. NGFS — Network of Central Banks and Supervisors for Greening the Financial System; d. TCFD — Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Financial Secretary, sets the responsible investment framework and guiding principles, which are implemented by the Exchange Fund Investment Office in the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The primary guiding principle is to enable the HKMA to give priority to ESG investments with long-term risk-adjusted returns comparable to those of other projects, so as to fulfil the investment objectives of the Exchange Fund. Details of the HKMA's responsible investment framework are set out on the HKMA website. The Investment Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, is responsible for overseeing the ESG and climate-related risks involved in the Exchange Fund's investment projects. The Investment Committee reviews the responsible investment framework and risk management approach, and monitors the progress of investments integrating ESG factors and the ESG status of the Exchange Fund through regular reports at meetings of the Risk Management and Surveillance Division of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. As shown in Figure 1, the ESG Committee established under the Exchange Fund Investment Office, chaired by the Chief Risk Officer, is responsible for coordinating and monitoring the various ESG initiatives of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. The motions discussed and the progress of work at each meeting of the ESG Committee are reported to the Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. Responsible Investment Monitoring and Governance Structure: The dedicated teams of the Risk Management and Surveillance Division work closely with the various investment teams of the Exchange Fund Investment Office on the integration of ESG factors, and assist the senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office in managing the ESG and climate-related risks and opportunities of various investment projects: Public Market Investments — The Credit, Regulations and Surveillance Committee, comprising the senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, monitors the ESG status of the fixed-income asset portfolio through regular reports from the Risk Management and Surveillance Division. In addition, the Risk Management and Surveillance Division also participates in the selection, appointment and monitoring process of external investment managers for the equity portfolio from an ESG perspective (for details, see the section "Striving to Actively Exercise Asset Ownership" in the "Risk Management" part on page 27). Private Market Investments — The Investment Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, considers the ESG-related assessments made by the Risk Management and Surveillance Division and the private market investment teams on each investment proposal. Concrete evidence² continues to show that the impact of climate change and related risks is significant. According to the latest report³ of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (the "Convention on Climate Change"), even assuming full fulfilment of the "Nationally Determined Contributions" targets announced by various regions, it is estimated that by 2100 the rise in global temperatures will still reach as high as 2.1 to 2.4 degrees Celsius, making it difficult to achieve the goal of the Paris Agreement to limit the rise in global average temperatures to well below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Should various regions adopt more aggressive policy measures to narrow the temperature gap, the resulting transition risks⁴ and the asset repricing by the market based on anticipated future trends, together with the inherent physical risks, would all intensify the pressure on asset valuation. In view of the updates to the global warming trajectory and model assumptions, the HKMA, drawing on the expertise of external consultants, further assessed the resilience of the Exchange Fund's "portfolio" under the "rapid transition" scenario (Figure 2), in addition to the scenarios assessed in 2021. The "rapid transition" scenario contains higher transition risk factors in the short, medium and long term, in which it is assumed that policy changes and technological developments jointly drive a rapid decline in carbon emissions, while various assets are suddenly divested in order to keep the rise in average temperatures within 1.5 degrees Celsius before 2100. This scenario is broadly consistent with the disorderly scenario recommended by the NGFS for forward-looking climate impact assessment. The "portfolio" is able to remain resilient in the medium to long term, because a relatively large proportion of its asset allocation belongs to sovereign bonds that are less sensitive to transition impacts. Sector distribution is key. Low-carbon electricity and renewable energy assets can benefit from the relevant transition. Transition risks and asset repricing may cause an impact on performance (especially equity assets) in the short term. The "portfolio" as a whole will suffer increasingly intensified impacts from physical risks that gradually emerge over time. Energy and traditional utilities remain the sectors most susceptible to impact. Climate scenarios, like the analyses of other modelling approaches, have their limitations. The relevant analysis is based on the market benchmark sector distribution at the strategic asset allocation level, and does not take into account the effect of actively selecting specific securities within a particular sector. From more in-depth research, it can be seen that the investment projects within the "portfolio" are generally more resilient to transition shocks or suffer milder impacts compared with the market benchmark of the strategic asset allocation. This result once again affirms that the HKMA's responsible investment focused on combating climate change can enhance the resilience of the asset portfolio. The trajectory of climate change remains uncertain, and scenario analysis methods will continue to evolve as data quality improves and policies develop. The HKMA will regularly review the relevant scenarios and refine its assessments in order to more clearly ascertain the resilience of the Exchange Fund to climate change. As a long-term investor, the HKMA fully understands the risks and opportunities that climate change can bring. The HKMA is committed to further expanding sustainable investment and seizing opportunities to address climate transition, mitigate climate risk and enhance the long-term returns of the asset portfolio. The HKMA continued its good momentum in 2022, increasing its holdings of green, social and sustainability bonds by a further 50%. In terms of equity investments, the HKMA invests in an actively managed equity portfolio themed on governance, and adopts a decarbonisation strategy favouring low-carbon-emission companies for its passive equity portfolio. In addition, the HKMA is exploring with the dedicated general partners of the Exchange Fund's "Long-Term Growth Portfolio" the establishment of a dedicated private equity portfolio to promote green and sustainable development in the Asian region (Figure 3). The HKMA has invested in a pan-African wind farm operator which, in addition to producing clean energy, also attaches great importance to social and natural biodiversity factors. Before the establishment of the wind farm, local villagers used poison bait to prevent predators from preying on their livestock, but this inadvertently endangered certain vultures that are an endangered species. Livestock is an important property of the local villagers; to help villagers protect their livestock, the operator built livestock shelters within the wind farm to protect the livestock from natural predators. In addition, the operator also employed a bird monitoring team to issue warnings when vultures were found attracted by carcasses of animals left behind by predators, so as to shut down the wind turbines and prevent the vultures from being struck by the blades. Reducing livestock predation brings a win-win situation: on the one hand it safeguards the livelihoods of the villagers, and on the other hand it reduces the deaths of vultures struck by wind turbines, thereby protecting the endangered species. Good ESG practices can bring more business opportunities to enterprises and open up sources of revenue, and the following supply chain-related operation is one such example. The investee company is an integrated logistics and warehousing operator in Mainland China, specialising in cold-chain pharmaceutical, chemical product and high-end consumer goods logistics services. The company faces continually rising ESG operating standards, mainly arising from multinational enterprise customers requiring their service providers to achieve high decarbonisation targets in line with the Paris Agreement. In response to the relevant demand, the company engaged external consultants to help formulate a "Three-Year ESG Plan" to reduce carbon emission intensity by 50% by 2030. This comprehensive decarbonisation plan already brought significant results in 2021 alone. The above ESG measures enabled the company to be awarded the "Low-Carbon Green Management Case" by the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing. These achievements and commendations enabled the company to gain considerable business opportunities from multinational corporate customers in the consumer and chemical products sectors that particularly value ESG practices. The growth of ESG investment is closely related to the development of the green and sustainable finance ecosystem. The HKMA actively cooperates with like-minded investors and partners to promote responsible investment and enhance industry skills. In 2022, the HKMA successfully held its 4th annual ESG workshop, exchanging good ESG practices with 9 participating private market institutions (including dedicated general partners, limited partners and enterprises), and promoting sustainable investment opportunities in the Asia-Pacific region and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. The HKMA is committed to reducing the carbon footprint of its own organisation, with the goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier, and contributing to Hong Kong's overall climate targets. On one hand, the HKMA strives to promote environmental sustainability, and on the other hand, it fulfils its commitment to caring for the physical and mental well-being of its staff, encouraging financial inclusion, and discharging its social responsibilities. The HKMA is dedicated to conducting its daily operations in a responsible and sustainable manner. To this end, the HKMA puts sustainable development into practice under the three pillars of environment, staff and social responsibility (Figure 1). The Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee is responsible for leading the HKMA in formulating and implementing its sustainability strategy. Chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, the Committee's members include three Deputy Chief Executives, as well as representatives from the Risk and Compliance Department and the Corporate Development and Operations Department; it submits regular reports to the Governance Sub-Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee. Under the Committee's leadership, various teams and working groups are responsible for planning and implementing measures in their respective areas. In 2022, the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee approved the climate targets for the organisation's operations and reviewed the transition roadmap for achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. During the year, the Committee continued to review the progress of the HKMA's green initiatives, including recommendations to strengthen the HKMA's sustainable procurement policies, procedures and methodologies. Sustainability Governance Structure HKMA Corporate Sustainability Journey In recognition of the HKMA's commitment to caring for the environment, its staff and society as a whole, the Hong Kong Council of Social Service awarded the HKMA the "15 Years Plus Caring Organisation" logo for the 16th consecutive year. The HKMA pays close attention to the carbon footprint of its own organisation and has formulated internal "Green Office Guidelines" to manage and control the environmental impact of its operational processes. The HKMA has incorporated environmental factors into the interior design, operation and maintenance of its offices. In 2022, BEAM Plus awarded the HKMA a Gold rating for certain renovated office areas. This was the second green building certification obtained after receiving the LEED Gold certification in 2021. Awarded BEAM Plus Interiors Version 1.0 Gold The HKMA has implemented a number of energy-saving measures. Total energy consumption in 2022 was 4,996.4 MWh (2.8 MWh per person), a decrease of 24.4% from 2015 (Figure 1). Total Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions in 2022 were 2,996.4 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2e) (1.7 tCO2e per person), a reduction of 38.2% from 2015 (Figure 2). In addition, the HKMA has implemented a print management system under which staff must log in to the printer to confirm each print request, helping to reduce unnecessary printouts and toner usage. Where printing is genuinely necessary, double-sided printing and black-and-white printing are also encouraged. The HKMA is also preparing to implement an internal electronic recordkeeping system. Total paper consumption in 2022 was 20.5 tonnes (0.0114 tonnes per person), a reduction of 65.3% from 2015 (Figure A). Figure A: Paper Intensity The HKMA's waste management efforts continue to adhere to the "4R" principle. In addition to conventional waste, the HKMA also reduces electronics waste by adopting technological solutions such as server virtualisation and private cloud infrastructure. In 2022, the HKMA engaged an external company to conduct a waste audit for the first time, analysing the composition of waste generated by its offices. The audit found that food waste accounted for a large proportion of total waste, and the HKMA therefore launched a food waste recycling programme (see "Enhancing Waste Management" on page 41). Total non-hazardous waste generated in 2022 (including general refuse and recyclables) was 242.0 tonnes (0.135 tonnes per person), a reduction of 4.8% from 2015 (Figure 3). The fluctuating trend was mainly due to the work-from-home arrangements implemented during the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic and the resumption of office operations after the fifth wave. Figure 3 Non-Hazardous Waste Intensity The HKMA gives top priority to waste reduction at source, and is committed to reducing, reusing and recycling. In 2022, the HKMA engaged a company to conduct a waste audit for the first time in order to gain a clearer understanding of the composition of waste generated in its daily operations (plastics, paper, metal, glass, wood, electronics, etc.) and to provide waste reduction recommendations. Based on the results of this audit, the HKMA launched a food waste recycling programme in November, setting up food waste collection bins in all pantries. The food waste collected each day is transported to an organic resources recovery centre in Hong Kong, where it is converted into renewable energy for electricity generation. The residues produced during the conversion process can also be made into compost for landscaping and agricultural staple food production. In addition, recycling bins are placed at various locations in the office for convenient use. The HKMA shares recycling tips with staff and pays greater attention to further improving the source separation of recyclables, as well as the points to note when handling recyclable items such as cardboard boxes and cartons, food containers and beverage bottles. Furthermore, we continue to organise activities to raise staff's environmental awareness, explain waste management policies, and encourage staff to make good use of the recycling facilities in the office.
